title: dQwen3.5: Hybrid-Attention Diffusion Language Models
author: Anton Xue et al
topic: diffusion models, autoregressive models, hybrid architectures
description: Diffusion language models generate text by iteratively unmasking positions in any order, and a cheap way to obtain one is to adapt a pretrained autoregressive model by making its causal attention bidirectional and continuing training with a masked diffusion objective. The problem this paper addresses is that modern autoregressive models increasingly use hybrid architectures, such as Qwen3.5, which interleaves three causal Gated DeltaNet recurrent layers with each attention layer, and unlike attention, these recurrent layers are causal by construction and cannot be made bidirectional just by removing a mask. The paper's contribution is to show that such hybrids can still be adapted: it bidirectionalizes only the minority attention layers, leaves the recurrent majority causal, and uses standard adaptation tools like token shifting (so each hidden state still predicts the next token, preserving the pretrained readout) and repurposed special tokens, releasing the resulting dQwen3.5 family along with a trunk-matched full-attention control for studying hybrid adaptation. The theoretical justification is that the apparent conflict between causal recurrence and any-order generation may be overstated, because natural language has a strong left-to-right bias in which the most predictive information lies in the immediately preceding tokens, and even full-attention diffusion models tend to decode globally left to right. The authors formalize this with an "anchor token" view, factorizing the sequence distribution as q(x_A) times the product over non-anchor positions of q(x_i | x_<i, x_A), where a small set A of tokens (for example, a later noun or verb that disambiguates an earlier phrase) carries all the non-causal dependence. Under this view, the causal recurrent layers can model ordinary prefix dependence while a few bidirectional attention layers only need to route information from these sparse future anchors, and because the intervention changes information flow in only a minority of layers, the pretrained structure is largely preserved, which suggests hybrids may be naturally efficient starting points for adaptation.

title: BARD: Bridging AutoRegressive and Diffusion Vision-Language Models Via Highly Efficient Progressive Block Merging and Stage-Wise Distillation
author: Baoyou Chen et al
topic: diffusion models, autoregressive models, progressive block merging, stage-wise distillation
description: Autoregressive vision-language models are strong but decode one token at a time, and while diffusion VLMs can refine many tokens in parallel within a block, directly converting a pretrained autoregressive VLM into a large-block diffusion model causes severe quality loss because the decoding pattern and the optimization problem change too abruptly. BARD addresses this by first converting the autoregressive checkpoint into a small-block (block size 4) diffusion "anchor" that already operates in the diffusion regime but stays close to the original model, then progressively doubling the block size (4, 8, 16, 32) so that each stage only merges two neighboring blocks from the previous stage rather than learning an entirely new decoding pattern. Throughout this progression the corruption process and the same-position denoising target stay fixed and only block granularity changes, which lets the model reuse prediction and reasoning patterns learned at smaller blocks. After each enlargement stage, the model is distilled from the fixed small-block anchor rather than from the original autoregressive model, because autoregressive logits predict the next token from clean causal prefixes while diffusion logits predict the same position from corrupted states, making their distributions fundamentally misaligned, whereas the anchor shares the student's diffusion formulation and provides a directly comparable teacher signal. The authors also introduce a mixed noise scheduler that interpolates between clean tokens, uniformly random visible tokens, and mask tokens, so the model learns not only to fill in masked positions but also to correct visibly wrong tokens, enabling a confidence-based inference rule where low-confidence tokens remain revisable. Finally, a memory-friendly packed layout stores the multimodal context once followed by the clean and noisy responses, with an attention mask that lets each noisy block see only the shared context, the preceding clean blocks, and itself, which prevents information leakage while avoiding duplication of the costly visual tokens.

title: Data-Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Models via On-Policy Distillation
author: Xingyu Su et al
topic: diffusion models, autoregressive models, on-policy distillation
description: Converting a pretrained autoregressive language model (ARLM) into a diffusion language model (DLM) is typically done by swapping causal attention for bidirectional attention and continuing training with a masked-diffusion objective, but this introduces two mismatches: the change of objective can erode knowledge the ARLM acquired through next-token prediction, and training on uniformly random masked states differs from the states the model actually visits at inference, where a confidence-guided sampler unmasks tokens along its own reverse trajectory. The authors address both issues with OPDLM, which adapts on-policy distillation (training a student on states sampled from its own generation process, with token-level supervision from a teacher) to ARLM-to-DLM conversion. Their theoretical framing casts block diffusion training as a generalized objective over a trajectory distribution, a state-selection distribution along each trajectory, a time weighting, and a per-position target distribution, which recovers the standard masked-diffusion loss as the special case of forward random-masking trajectories with hard one-hot targets and makes clear that the training-inference mismatch lives entirely in the choice of trajectory distribution. OPDLM therefore replaces the forward masking trajectories with the student's own sampler-induced reverse decoding trajectories, supervising intermediate states actually encountered at inference, and replaces hard labels with soft targets from the original frozen ARLM, which retains the base model's full predictive knowledge without requiring a separately trained DLM teacher. The key technical trick resolving the state-space mismatch between a teacher that reads clean causal prefixes and a student that reads partially masked blocks is to query the ARLM on the causal prefix of the student's own terminal generated sequence for each masked position, yielding a KL-based self-distillation in which teacher and student share the same weights and differ only in attention mask. A rollout-length curriculum that gradually lengthens on-policy generations stabilizes early training, when the freshly converted student produces unreliable long rollouts, and the overall result reframes ARLM-to-DLM conversion as a lightweight post-training procedure rather than a costly continued-pretraining stage.

title: Locally Coherent Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
author: Michael Hersche et al
topic: diffusion models, block diffusion, parallel decoding
description: Diffusion language models promise sub-linear generation latency by unmasking many tokens per step, but because standard masked diffusion samples each token independently from its conditional marginal, parallel decoding ignores dependencies among tokens generated in the same step and produces incoherent local structures like broken multi-token words or invalid code syntax. The paper's first contribution is to generalize discrete diffusion from individual tokens to contiguous blocks of tokens that are modeled jointly, replacing the usual conditional token independence assumption with a weaker conditional block independence assumption. Theoretically, the authors prove that the smallest achievable NELBO under block independence is strictly lower than under token independence, with the gap exactly equal to the total correlation within each block, so larger blocks reduce the irreducible modeling error. Because directly modeling a joint distribution over blocks is intractable (the space grows exponentially with block size), their method, CoDiLA, pairs the bidirectional DLM, which supplies global context and per-token marginals, with a small auxiliary autoregressive model that decodes each short block sequentially, keeping AR latency bounded by the block size rather than the full sequence length. A second theorem justifies the interface between the two models: conditioning the AR model on the full marginals is sufficient to recover any target joint distribution, whereas truncating to top-k tokens restricts the solution to a constrained Fréchet class that can provably exclude the most likely coherent sequence. The authors therefore use soft-conditioning, feeding the AR model the expected token embeddings under the DLM's marginals wrapped in boundary tokens, which retains the full distributional signal in a form a pretrained AR model can use while preserving the DLM's bidirectional capabilities like any-order generation and infilling across blocks.

title: TEAM: Temporal-Spatial Consistency Guided Expert Activation for MoE Diffusion Language Model Acceleration
author: Linye Wei et al
topic: diffusion models, mixture-of-experts, expert activation, acceleration
description: Mixture-of-Experts diffusion language models suffer from a fundamental mismatch: because every token in a decoding block is processed in parallel at each denoising step and each token routes to its own experts, a single forward pass activates a large fraction of all experts even though only a few tokens end up exceeding the confidence threshold and being accepted, which effectively reverts the model to dense-model memory and latency costs. The authors ground their solution, TEAM, in the observation that block-wise diffusion decoding differs from ordinary batched inference by exhibiting temporal consistency (the same block is reprocessed across iterations, and accepted tokens stop changing yet keep triggering expert activations) and spatial consistency (masked tokens share an identical mask embedding differing only in positional encoding, so their routing concentrates on a small shared subset of experts). For decoded tokens, TEAM uses delayed caching, computing an accepted token for only one additional forward pass, since its hidden state changes most right after acceptance and is approximately stable afterward, and then reusing its cached key-value pairs with no periodic refresh, a choice justified by the near-autoregressive decoding order inherited from autoregressive initialization. Masked tokens are split into hot tokens, which either have fairly high confidence or sit close to already decoded positions and are therefore likely to be accepted soon, and cold tokens, which are distant and low-confidence and so are likely to be remasked anyway. For hot tokens, TEAM performs speculative exploration by building several branches that additionally accept the top-confidence candidates and verifying them in parallel, which is prohibitive for dense models but well suited to MoE because the extra branches raise the low arithmetic intensity of already-loaded experts while their similarity means few new experts get activated. For cold tokens, a double-round routing scheme first determines the necessary expert set from newly accepted and hot tokens, then restricts cold tokens to route only within that set, eliminating wasteful token-specific activations while still leaving open the chance that a cold token is unexpectedly accepted later.

title: DreamReasoner-8B: Block-Size Curriculum Learning for Diffusion Reasoning Models
author: Zirui Wu et al
topic: diffusion models, block diffusion, curriculum learning, reasoning
description: Block diffusion language models factor a sequence autoregressively across contiguous blocks while denoising the tokens within each block in parallel through bidirectional masked diffusion, which offers a tunable trade-off between the sequential coherence of autoregressive decoding and the parallelism of diffusion. The core problem is that larger blocks, which promise more parallelism, put heavy pressure on the model to maintain sequential fidelity inside each block, and it has been unclear whether such models can be trained to carry out long chain-of-thought reasoning at coarse granularity. The authors argue that training directly on large blocks leads the model to rely on parallel, long-range aggregation within each block instead of learning to break reasoning into fine-grained, locally causal steps, whereas small-block training builds a token-level causal scaffold that can naturally extend to decoding over larger blocks. Their central contribution, block-size curriculum learning, exploits this asymmetry by first fine-tuning with small blocks to acquire robust local dependencies and then moving to larger or mixed block sizes, so the model gains coarse-grained parallelism without losing fine-grained precision and a single model can serve many inference block sizes. They instantiate this in DreamReasoner-8B, an open block-diffusion reasoning model built by continually pretraining an autoregressive checkpoint under a block-diffusion objective and then applying the curriculum during supervised fine-tuning, which treats block size as a deployment-time setting that trades quality against efficiency rather than a fixed architectural constant. Finally, they note that standard confidence-threshold decoding is overly conservative because contiguous spans often stabilize before each token individually crosses the threshold, so they introduce RelaxedConfidence, which lowers a token's commitment threshold in proportion to how many nearby positions are already decoded or highly confident, letting well-supported spans be committed earlier while isolated tokens still face the full threshold.

title: Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
author: Alex M. Tseng et al
topic: mixture-of-experts, expert pruning, higher-order interactions
description: Mixture-of-Experts language models must keep every expert in GPU memory even though each token activates only a few, so their large parameter counts create a serious memory bottleneck, and expert pruning (permanently removing whole experts without retraining) is the most direct remedy. Existing pruning methods such as REAP, EAN, MAN, and Frequency are all first-order: they give each expert an independent scalar importance score, implicitly assuming that experts contribute additively, even though experts are routinely co-selected and work cooperatively, so removing one expert can disrupt the circuits its partners depend on. The paper introduces HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), which is the first theoretically derived pruning objective that explicitly accounts for pairwise interactions between experts. Building on the substitution-error decomposition from REAP, the authors observe that the squared substitution error, unlike a linear score, contains cross terms between pruned experts, and they define a tractable surrogate Z (the squared total gate-weighted output norm of the pruned experts that were active for a token) that depends only on observable quantities rather than on the unknown replacement experts. Theorem 1 shows that the squared substitution error is bounded above by a constant factor (1 plus the ratio of maximum to minimum expert output norms, squared) times Z, so minimizing Z provably reduces an upper bound on the pruning error, and Theorem 2 shows that minimizing the calibration-set expectation of Z is equivalent to a binary quadratic program over an interaction matrix F whose diagonal holds individual expert contributions and whose off-diagonal entries hold co-contributions of expert pairs, with high entries meaning that pruning both experts together is especially costly. REAP emerges as a special case of HOPE in which the off-diagonal terms are ignored, since the diagonal of F differs from the squared REAP score only by the variance of an expert's contribution, so any added benefit is attributable to the interaction terms, and the method remains practical because it needs just one calibration forward pass to build a per-layer F matrix and solves each layer's quadratic program via a continuous relaxation that is rounded to the top entries at negligible extra cost.

title: GrowMTP: Can RL Grow its Own Draft Head?
author: Minghua He et al
topic: reinforcement learning, speculative decoding, draft heads
description: GrowMTP addresses the fact that reinforcement learning post-training of language models is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, and that speculative decoding, the standard remedy, requires a draft head that has already been pretrained or warmed up offline, which adds a training cost outside the RL run and leaves models without such a head with no route to acceleration. The central insight is that RL itself supplies the two things online draft-head training needs: a rollout distribution far narrower than pretraining's, so the head only has to fit one task distribution, and a verification step that already produces target distributions and acceptance decisions that would otherwise be discarded. Since the first draft position always yields valid supervision, a randomly initialized head can begin learning immediately, and all head updates are detached from the policy backbone so the original RL objective is left untouched. To keep training consistent with rollout-time drafting, the method uses Draft-Path Reconstruction, which records each cycle's context and drafts and feeds those drafts back in order, so every target distribution is paired with a head distribution under the same draft-conditioned state; this avoids the bias of teacher forcing, which trains the head on committed tokens that match the drafting state only when the whole preceding prefix was accepted, a mismatch that worsens with depth. The second contribution is the Depth-Coupled Acceptance loss, which starts from the fact that a draft at depth k only counts if all earlier drafts are accepted, so the expected accepted length is a chain of products of per-position acceptance rates (one minus total variation distance), and it applies a logarithm to this chain surrogate to give cycles with smaller chain values more relative gradient weight, while the gradient at each position is naturally weighted by the acceptance overlaps of the preceding drafts. Because this soft weighting still lets positions after a rejection receive gradient even though those drafts condition on tokens that were never committed, the third contribution, verify-gated masking, truncates the chain sum at and including the first rejected position, so supervision depth self-paces with the realized accepted prefix and needs no warm-up or depth schedule.

title: Temporal Self-Distillation: Faster Inference in Discrete Language Models
author: Shijian Xu et al
topic: diffusion models, self-distillation, inference efficiency
description: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) can in principle commit several tokens per forward pass, but pushing parallel decoding too aggressively sharply degrades output quality, because the model's predictions at early denoising steps, made with mostly masked context, are unreliable for the tokens being committed. Existing remedies either design adaptive decoding schedules that only choose which positions are safe to unmask, which stay limited by the quality of early predictions, or use offline distillation that first generates full teacher trajectories and then trains a separate student in a costly two-stage pipeline decoupled from the student's own behavior. The paper proposes Temporal Self-Distillation (TSD), an on-policy objective that closes the gap between early and final predictions by using the model itself as its own teacher across time: for each masked position along a sampled denoising trajectory, the model's early-step distribution is trained to match its own stop-gradient distribution at the timestep when that position is eventually committed, which is conditioned on a more complete decoded context. Because Fast-dLLM style decoding is unmasking-only, each position has a unique commitment time, so the target is well defined and specific to that token, and the teacher signal comes from the model's own rollouts, so no offline data, separate teacher checkpoint, or two-stage training is required, and the method applies equally to base and RL post-trained policies. The objective is made practical by sampling a single timestep per trajectory, which gives an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of the timestep-averaged loss while requiring gradients at only one step, and by using a bounded, symmetric Jensen-Shannon divergence instead of KL, which is asymmetric and unbounded and can produce unstable updates when teacher probabilities are small. Trajectories are additionally weighted by a verifier of the final outcome so that unsuccessful rollouts do not reinforce their predictions, with a length-aware variant that favors shorter correct solutions since these naturally need fewer decoding steps, and this reward is used only as a weight rather than as a policy-optimization objective, which distinguishes TSD from RL-style methods and from concurrent self-distillation work that builds targets from unnormalized stage-level signals or averages over all future steps.

title: Fixed State, Long Reach: What a Constant-Size Cache Buys Block Diffusion at Scale
author: Vaibhav Singh et al
topic: block diffusion, caching, state-space models, Mamba
description: Diffusion language models decode many tokens in parallel, but their bidirectional denoiser rules out the standard key-value cache used in autoregressive inference, so each denoising step recomputes over the whole sequence. Block diffusion partially fixes this by generating blocks left to right with diffusion inside each block, so finalized blocks form a clean prefix that can be cached, but existing block caches are built for attention backbones, which means memory grows linearly with context and compute stays quadratic. Many of these caches are also training-free retrofits onto full-attention models, so they only approximate the true bidirectional computation rather than reproducing what the model learned. The paper's central insight is that block diffusion only requires finalized blocks to be summarized into a reusable state, so any sequence mixer with such a state qualifies, and state-space models like Mamba are a natural fit because their recurrent hidden state is a fixed-size summary of the past regardless of prefix length. To make the cache exact, the authors train with a single-frontier block-causal objective that matches decode-time conditions (clean earlier blocks, a partially masked frontier block, fully masked future blocks), enforced in Mamba layers by running the forward recurrence over the whole prefix while confining the backward scan to the frontier block so no information leaks from the masked future. Their contribution is a unified cached decoding interface that exposes the attention KV-cache, the O(1) Mamba conv-plus-SSM state, and a hybrid of the two, along with a controlled study of three denoisers that differ only in the sequence mixer, arguing that the constant-size state gives constant per-step cost and that its position-free recurrence should also make the model more robust to lengths beyond those seen in training, whereas attention meets unseen positions and prefix lengths.

title: Efficient One-to-Many Translation with Joint Multi-Stream Diffusion
author: Yiwen Guan et al
topic: one-to-many translation, multi-stream diffusion, language-agnostic
description: One-to-many machine translation, as needed in live interpreting where the set of requested target languages changes dynamically, is costly for autoregressive systems because decoding must happen token by token and separately for each target language, so latency grows linearly with both sequence length and the number of targets. Existing non-autoregressive methods parallelize tokens but assume conditional independence among them, which causes the multimodality problem, and they are designed for one-to-one translation, so adapting them to many targets means running multiple memory-hungry models. The paper proposes PrismDiff, a discrete masked diffusion framework that refines all target languages in parallel on a single shared canvas, with a single model replacing multiple independent systems. Its central idea is a language-agnostic semantic anchor: instead of conditioning on source tokens, which ties the model to one source language, the diffusion process is conditioned on continuous hidden states from a frozen multilingual sentence encoder (LaBSE) passed through a learned linear projection, so any source language mapped into that shared space can in principle be used without retraining. The canvas concatenates the anchor with K noisy target streams, each using its own language-specific mask token, and uses exclusive attention within each stream so that languages do not interfere, while shared parameters and joint optimization give implicit cross-lingual regularization. Reset positional encoding restarts position indices at zero for each stream, which lets target languages be reordered, added, or removed flexibly, and inference uses a logarithm-uniform remasking schedule so the number of sampling steps becomes a knob for trading quality against latency without changing model capacity, along with CTC-style collapse of repeated tokens to compensate for the lack of autoregressive constraints.

title: Structured Transforms for Low-Overhead Quantization of Language Models
author: Daria Cherniuk et al
topic: weight quantization, Kashin decomposition, discrete cosine transform
description: Prior work applied Kashin decomposition to LLM weight quantization by writing each weight vector as w = u + Pv̂, where P is orthogonal and both u and v̂ have small infinity norm, which yields four-peaked distributions well suited to 2-bit clustering. That approach had three weaknesses: its matrix-wise reformulation lost the per-vector convergence guarantees of Kashin's original theorem, the four-peak structure was not reliably produced, and cluster centers were found with costly multi-restart k-means. This paper keeps the vector-level formulation, where rigorous proofs exist, and replaces the dense random orthogonal matrix with a sign-randomized Discrete Cosine Transform, so P z = IDCT(ε ⊙ DCT(z)) needs no stored N×N matrix and costs O(N log N) per iteration instead of O(N²). Its main algorithmic contribution is a Greedy Algorithm with Alternating Updates, which fixes the update schedule in blocks of four steps, two greedy steps from the cube-vertex dictionary (accumulating into u) followed by two from the DCT-rotated dictionary (accumulating into v̂), building on the recent acceleration of Kashin's theorem by Kashin and coauthors. The theory shows that one block contracts the residual norm by a factor (1 − β(N))^(1/2) with β(N) = α²(N)/36, giving geometric decay over blocks and an infinity-norm bound of order (log N)² (log log N)¹² / √N on both factors, which is slightly weaker than the unconstrained adaptive scheme but within polylogarithmic factors of it. The proof sketch works by cases on which half of the dictionary is "good" for the residual, using the fact that consecutive greedy updates are orthogonal so that any wasted steps on the wrong half have bounded combined contribution, and then applying the triangle inequality. The fixed schedule is worth this price because each factor's first two updates add ±c1 and ±c2 determined by residual norms, so the four peak locations are analytically ±c1 ± c2, which guarantees the four-peak distributions and allows closed-form initialization of the cluster centers, eliminating multi-restart k-means and leaving only a few refinement iterations, with the method then composed with OPTQ-style error compensation and QuIP-style incoherence preprocessing.

title: Osprey: Target-agnostic Pre-training Makes Stronger Drafters in Speculative Decoding
author: Fengxiang Bie et al
topic: speculative decoding, pretraining, distillation
description: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by having a lightweight drafter propose tokens that a larger target model verifies in parallel, but drafters are usually trained on a narrow data distribution for one specific target, so their proposals become poorly aligned with the target when the workload shifts. This is ironic because target models are valued for the broad generalization they gain from large-scale pretraining, while the drafters that accelerate them do not inherit that benefit. Pretraining drafters has been hard because existing designs such as EAGLE consume the target's hidden states and are distilled on its outputs, which ties them to a single target and forces the whole expensive pipeline to be repeated for each new one. Osprey addresses this by splitting training into a target-agnostic phase done once and a lightweight per-target adaptation phase: it prunes an off-the-shelf pretrained small language model to its embeddings, language-modeling head, and a few early layers (since a deep drafter would erase the latency gains), then restores the pruned model's next-token prediction ability by continuing pretraining on generic text, yielding a reusable backbone that carries a broad language prior. To adapt this backbone to a given target, Osprey resizes the embedding and output head to the target vocabulary, initializing new rows from the mean of the corresponding source-token rows so that pretrained knowledge is retained, and it expands the attention QKV projections with zero-initialized columns so the drafter can take in projected multi-layer target hidden states without initially disturbing the pretrained computation, since the new inputs contribute nothing at the start and the model behaves exactly as the pretrained backbone. Finally, all drafter weights are trained by distilling the frozen target's output distribution using EAGLE-3's training-time-test unrolling with a discounted loss that emphasizes earlier drafting steps, so each deployed drafter is target-specific while inheriting a reusable, broadly trained foundation, and the paper's core contribution is this decoupled recipe that separates general language modeling from target conditioning rather than proposing a new distillation objective.

title: Representation-based Masked Diffusion Model
author: Yangrong Hu et al
topic: diffusion models, masked language modeling, latent variables
description: Masked diffusion models generate text in parallel by sampling every masked token independently given the visible context, which amounts to approximating the true joint distribution over masked positions with a product of per-token marginals. This is a poor fit for language, where masked tokens remain strongly dependent through syntax, entity consistency, and long-range constraints, so aggressive parallelism yields outputs that are locally plausible but globally incoherent. The authors formalize this failure as the Conditional Dependency Gap, measured by the conditional total correlation (a KL divergence between the true joint over masked tokens and the product of their marginals given the unmasked context). Their proposed remedy, the Representation-based Masked Diffusion Model (RMDM), introduces a global latent variable z that acts as a common cause of the tokens, and they prove that the residual gap vanishes exactly when the masked tokens are conditionally independent given both the context and z, so that independent parallel sampling becomes exact in that case. To make z usable at generation time, where the ground-truth text and its encoder embedding do not exist, they use a two-stage design: a pretrained encoder supplies rich sequence-level semantic embeddings, and a MeanFlow model learns a one-step transport that maps the embedding distribution onto a standard Gaussian, so that z can simply be sampled once from the prior at inference and used to condition the masked diffusion denoiser (via adaptive layer normalization, with a low-dimensional bottleneck and noise injection to stabilize training), while the encoder and MeanFlow network are needed only to build training latents. The paper also gives a tri-part decomposition of the joint KL divergence between data and model into the mismatch between the MeanFlow-induced latent distribution and the Gaussian prior, the residual token dependencies left after conditioning on z, and the token-wise prediction error of the denoiser, which offers a principled account of why each component of the framework targets a distinct source of error in parallel decoding.

title: A Ticket from Marginals to Joins: Coupled-Noise Distillation for One-Step Block Generation in Diffusion Language Models
author: Lin Yao et al
topic: diffusion models, masked language modeling, distillation
description: Diffusion language models predict all tokens of a block in parallel, but a single forward pass samples each position from its own marginal distribution, so under token-wise cross-entropy the result is a product of marginals rather than the joint distribution of a coherent block. The masked inputs also offer no sample-specific variable that could select one joint mode, which is why autoregressive models (via the growing prefix), latent-variable models (via a latent z), and continuous diffusion (via initial noise) can coordinate tokens while a one-pass masked model cannot. The paper proposes giving the masked model an analogous input by adding a data-independent Gaussian noise field to its mask embeddings, so that one sampled field, called a ticket, should select one coherent block and different tickets should select different blocks. The difficulty is that this noise is only an auxiliary input rather than a corrupted encoding of the target, so no correspondence between noise and coherent continuations is given and must be learned. The proposed method, CONDOR, learns this coupling in two stages: winner-take-all supervision on real text, in which the model predicts masked tokens under several noise samples and only the best-fitting sample receives the ground-truth loss, lets different noise samples specialize to different continuations and establishes dependence on noise. For the remaining losing samples, an EMA teacher refines the student's own one-pass output over several decoding steps (keeping the highest leave-one-out-scored positions and filling the rest) while holding the same noise fixed, and the student is then distilled to reproduce that refined block in a single pass, thereby converting noise dependence into coherence. The novelty is that this is, to the authors' knowledge, the first discrete masked diffusion language model to generate a full block in one forward pass and the first from-scratch training recipe for it, requiring neither a target-side latent encoder nor an autoregressive teacher, and it extends to longer text through block-causal attention with fresh noise per block.

title: DFlow: Enabling Verifier Information Flow in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
author: Yaojie Zhang et al
topic: diffusion models, speculative decoding, information flow
description: Block diffusion speculative decoding has a small drafter propose a block of future tokens in parallel, then has the target model verify them in a single forward pass. Only the accepted prefix and a bonus token are committed, so the rejected suffix and the target model's hidden states at those positions are thrown away. The paper identifies this as an information discontinuity: in the next round, the drafter must re-predict positions that overlap with the discarded suffix, starting from plain mask embeddings even though the target model has already computed contextual representations for them. The core insight is that rejection is a decision about discrete token commitment, not a measure of whether the verifier's continuous representation is useful. Because each proposed position takes part in the target's causal computation, its hidden state can still carry predictive information about the continuation, even when the proposed token itself is wrong. Based on this, DFlow relays the verifier hidden states from the rejected suffix into the next drafting round at the corresponding overlapping positions, at no extra cost in target forward passes. To make them usable, it projects the states into the drafter's space with the same projection DFlash already uses, and shifts them by one position to reconcile the target's next-token prediction with the drafter's same-position mask prediction. Since these states were computed after the first rejected proposal while the next round continues from the target's bonus token, a lightweight MLP takes both boundary token embeddings and the relayed state and outputs channel-wise scaling and correction vectors, which let the model keep, suppress, or adjust the relayed information before adding it to the mask embedding. To teach the drafter to exploit this cross-round signal, the paper introduces Multi-Round Self-Conditioned Training, which unrolls consecutive draft-and-verify rounds so the training distribution matches inference, with round transitions guided by the target trajectory and gradients detached from verification and across rounds. The framework is also designed to combine with stronger drafters that model dependencies within a block, provided training uses an online rollout so the rejected suffix follows the same trajectory as at inference.

title: Prefix-Denoising Consistency: Test-Time Verification for Diffusion Language Models
author: Yuki Ichihara et al
topic: diffusion models, self-consistency, verification
description: Diffusion language models are usually decoded at low temperature, so repeated full generations tend to follow near-identical denoising trajectories, which means the agreement that autoregressive self-consistency relies on overstates reliability instead of giving an independent check, while prior temporal voting only reuses intermediate states from a single run and cannot branch away once that run locks into a wrong reasoning path. The paper proposes PDC (Prefix-Denoising Consistency), which takes one completed output, keeps an exact prefix at several keep rates (0.1, 0.5, 0.9), remasks the remaining positions within the same fixed-length window, and re-denoises them with the same model at the same temperature. The final answer is a majority vote over the regenerated answers only, with the initial answer deliberately excluded so that any improvement must come from the regenerations themselves. The novelty is treating prefix-conditioned regeneration as a black-box, diffusion-specific primitive that creates structured alternative trajectories, where weak conditioning lets most of the reasoning change, strong conditioning perturbs only the tail, and all of them preserve useful context from the original solution. The motivating premise is a reproduction gap, meaning that regeneration tends to preserve an initially correct answer more often than it repeats the same wrong answer, so reproducibility serves as an implicit verification signal. Theoretically, in a stylized binary-answer setting with conditionally independent regenerations, accuracy equals the prior probability of a correct initial answer times V3 of the retention rates plus the complementary term for wrong answers, where V3 is the probability that at least two of three Bernoulli events succeed, and PDC beats the initial answer exactly when the wrong answers it corrects outweigh the correct answers it spoils, with a sufficient condition being that retention is at least the same-wrong persistence at every keep rate and strictly greater at one, since V3 increases in each coordinate.

title: Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing for Mixture-of-Experts
author: Lean Wang et al
topic: load balancing, mixture-of-experts, transformers
description: Mixture-of-Experts models require balanced routing of tokens across experts to avoid routing collapse and computational bottlenecks, and the standard solution has been to add an auxiliary loss term that encourages balance but simultaneously injects gradients that interfere with the primary language modeling objective. The paper identifies this as an inherent dilemma, since a small auxiliary loss coefficient leaves load imbalanced while a large coefficient distorts the main training signal, meaning no single coefficient can fully satisfy both objectives at once. To escape this tradeoff, the authors propose Loss-Free Balancing, which instead of using a loss term, applies a per-expert additive bias to routing scores purely to influence the top-K selection during the forward pass, while leaving the actual gating weights used to combine expert outputs unaffected by this bias. The bias for each expert is updated after every batch based on whether that expert was recently overloaded or underused, so the mechanism steers routing toward balance through a control-like feedback loop rather than through a differentiable penalty, meaning it introduces no gradient interference with the language modeling loss. The design is also constructed to preserve the causal structure of autoregressive modeling, since biases are updated only from past batches rather than from information about the current sequence, which distinguishes it from alternative balancing approaches such as Expert Choice that leak future token information into earlier routing decisions. The core contribution is thus a reconceptualization of load balancing as a bias-correction control problem rather than a joint optimization objective, aiming to achieve balance without paying the performance cost normally associated with auxiliary losses.

title: Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models
author: Xin Cheng et al
topic: conditional memory, sparsity, large language models
description: The paper starts from the observation that Mixture-of-Experts models exploit conditional computation to scale capacity efficiently, but transformers otherwise lack any native mechanism for cheap knowledge lookup, forcing them to reconstruct static, formulaic information such as named entities through expensive layers of attention and feed-forward computation. To address this mismatch between the nature of language, which mixes dynamic reasoning with highly stereotyped local patterns, and the architecture used to model it, the authors propose treating conditional memory as a complementary sparsity axis alongside conditional computation. Their instantiation, Engram, modernizes classic N-gram embeddings with tokenizer compression, multi-head hashing, and a context-aware gating mechanism that uses the current hidden state to selectively accept or suppress the retrieved static embedding, addressing the inherent brittleness of naive hash-based lookups. They further formulate a Sparsity Allocation problem asking how a fixed parameter budget should be split between MoE experts and Engram memory slots, motivated by the idea that computation and lookup serve fundamentally different linguistic needs and should not be treated as substitutes for each other in either direction. The architecture is also designed around the insight that, unlike MoE routing which depends on runtime hidden states, lookup indices are known purely from input token identities, making retrieval deterministic and therefore prefetchable ahead of time from slower memory tiers. Altogether the work proposes a new modeling primitive intended to relieve the network's computational depth from redundant memorization, freeing capacity for genuine reasoning and long-context processing.

title: PowerAttention: Exponentially Scaling of Receptive Fields for Effective Sparse Attention
author: Lida Chen et al
topic: sparse attention, graph theory, transformer architecture
description: The paper addresses a limitation of sparse attention methods used to reduce the quadratic cost of transformer attention over long contexts, namely that existing static sparsity patterns either fail to cover the full context or expand their usable receptive field too slowly across layers. The authors formalize this by modeling attention patterns as directed acyclic graphs, where a token's receptive field is the set of positions reachable within a fixed number of layers, and show that patterns like sliding window attention grow this field only linearly with depth while others like dilated attention leave permanent gaps in coverage. Building on this graph-theoretic framework, they propose PowerAttention, which connects each token only to positions at power-of-two distances, and prove that this construction guarantees both a bounded out-degree per node and full reachability of any distance within a logarithmic number of layers. This design elegantly resolves the tension between sparsity and coverage: it keeps the same fixed attention budget per token as other sparse methods while making receptive field growth exponential rather than linear or gapped. The theoretical result directly explains why such a pattern should generalize better to long-range dependencies than heuristically designed alternatives, since it is derived from an explicit optimality argument about graph reachability under a degree constraint. Overall, the contribution is a principled, provably complete sparse attention pattern derived from information-flow theory rather than empirical trial and error, intended to serve as a foundation for future sparse attention designs.

title: Reducing Transformer Key-Value Cache Size with Cross-Layer Attention
author: William Brandon et al
topic: long-context attention, cross-layer sharing, key-value cache
description: Large language model inference is often bottlenecked by the memory required to store the key-value cache, and prior solutions like Multi-Query Attention and Grouped-Query Attention address this only by sharing key/value heads within a single layer. This paper introduces Cross-Layer Attention, which extends the sharing idea across layers instead, so that only a subset of layers compute fresh key/value projections while other layers reuse activations from earlier layers. The approach is motivated by the observation that KV sharing within a layer and across layers are orthogonal axes, meaning CLA can be freely combined with MQA or GQA to compound their memory savings. Conceptually, the method treats the sharing factor, the number of layers grouped under one KV projection, as a new tunable knob that trades off cache size against model expressiveness. This is a purely architectural intervention that leaves the core attention computation and system-level compatibility, such as tensor parallelism, largely intact, since shared layers still need to be re-read from memory during decoding. The core contribution is thus a conceptually simple generalization of existing head-sharing techniques into a new dimension of the transformer architecture, aimed at unlocking further KV cache reduction beyond what MQA and GQA alone can offer.

title: IndexCache: Accelerating Sparse Attention via Cross-Layer Index Reuse
author: Yushi Bai
topic: sparse attention, cross-layer sharing, indexer optimization
description: In DeepSeek Sparse Attention, the lightning indexer that picks each layer's top-k tokens still scores all preceding tokens at every layer, so its cost stays quadratic in sequence length and grows to dominate long-context inference even though core attention itself is cheap. The paper's core insight is that these per-layer top-k selections are highly redundant across neighboring layers, but this redundancy can't be exploited the way prior cross-layer sharing methods do, since those rely on full attention scores as an oracle, which DSA has already replaced with the lightweight indexer. IndexCache resolves this by designating a small subset of layers as Full layers that keep computing their own indices, while the rest become Shared layers that simply inherit the nearest Full layer's selected token indices, cutting total indexer computation with only a single added conditional branch at inference. To choose which layers should remain Full without any retraining, the authors introduce a greedy search that incrementally converts layers to Shared based on the resulting language modeling loss on a calibration set, since naive uniform interleaving turns out to remove some layers whose indices are much harder to substitute than others. For settings where retraining is feasible, they propose a multi-layer distillation loss that trains a retained indexer against the combined attention patterns of every layer it will serve, and they prove this objective is mathematically equivalent to distilling toward the centroid of those layers' attention distributions, giving a principled justification for why a single shared indexer can serve multiple layers well. Together these two approaches show that the sharing principle previously limited to full-attention oracles generalizes to sparse, indexer-based attention, and the authors argue the same idea should extend to other dynamic token-selection sparse attention schemes beyond DSA.

title: Geomtric Autoencoder for Diffusion Models
author: Hangyu Liu et al
topic: diffusion models, autoencoders, latent space design
description: Latent diffusion models rely on autoencoders whose latent spaces are typically designed heuristically, leaving unresolved tensions between semantic discriminability, reconstruction fidelity, and latent compactness. This paper introduces the Geometric Autoencoder (GAE) to address this by systematically analyzing where and how semantic guidance from Vision Foundation Models should be injected into the autoencoder, concluding that supervising directly at the compressed latent bottleneck (rather than at high-dimensional encoder features or through a re-expanded projection) best preserves semantic structure through compression. To make this bottleneck supervision dimensionally compatible, the authors propose a learned, spatially aware downsampler that distills a foundation model's high-dimensional features into a compact target representation for the autoencoder to match. A second contribution replaces the conventional KL-divergence regularization of VAEs with a parameter-free latent normalization that projects the latent mean onto a unit hypersphere, arguing this yields a more bounded, stable manifold better suited to diffusion training than the traditional Gaussian prior constraint. Third, the framework incorporates a dynamic noise-sampling mechanism during training, perturbing the normalized latent with variable-scale Gaussian noise so the decoder learns to reconstruct reliably across a range of noise intensities, which matters because diffusion sampling exposes the decoder to noisy latents unlike standard autoencoder training. Together these design choices are motivated by the idea that a principled, geometrically constrained and semantically anchored latent space removes ad hoc heuristics from prior alignment strategies and gives diffusion models an inherently more learnable manifold to model.

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
author: Joshua Ainslie et al
topic: multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, uptraining
description: Autoregressive Transformer decoding is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth, since every decoding step must reload all attention keys and values, and this cost grows with the number of key-value heads in standard multi-head attention. Multi-query attention had been proposed to fix this by collapsing all heads down to a single shared key and value head, but this aggressive reduction in capacity tends to hurt output quality and can destabilize training, and training a separate low-quality model purely for speed is often impractical anyway. The paper's first contribution is a recipe for uptraining: taking an existing multi-head checkpoint, mean-pooling its key and value projection matrices into a smaller number of heads, and then continuing pretraining for only a small fraction of the original compute budget, so that a fast variant can be obtained cheaply from a model already trained for quality rather than requiring a full separate training run. The second and more central contribution is grouped-query attention, which generalizes multi-query attention by partitioning query heads into groups that each share a single key and value head, so that the degree of key-value sharing can be tuned between the two extremes of full multi-head attention and single-head multi-query attention. The theoretical motivation is that as models scale up, the number of attention heads typically grows too, so cutting all the way down to one shared head becomes an increasingly disproportionate reduction in both memory bandwidth and representational capacity relative to the rest of the model; grouped-query attention lets the number of key-value heads scale down more gradually and proportionally instead. This is reinforced by the observation that memory bandwidth overhead from keys and values scales only with model dimension, while the model's overall parameters and computation scale with the square of that dimension, meaning larger models are relatively less bandwidth-bound to begin with, and by the fact that standard multi-device sharding replicates a single key-value head across partitions, so having more than one head avoids wasting that replicated capacity. Together, uptraining and grouped-query attention are proposed as a combined solution that converts existing multi-head checkpoints into models offering a tunable, more principled tradeoff between inference speed and representational quality than multi-query attention alone.

title: You Only Cache Once: Decoder-Decoder Architectures for Language Models
author: Yutao Sun
topic: long-context attention, decoder-decoder, efficient attention
description: As large language models are pushed to longer contexts, standard decoder-only Transformers become memory-bound because every layer must store its own key-value cache, and prefilling long inputs is slow since attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length. This paper introduces YOCO, a decoder-decoder architecture that splits the model into a self-decoder followed by a cross-decoder, where the self-decoder uses an efficient attention mechanism (with constant memory) to produce a single global key-value cache that all cross-decoder layers then reuse via cross-attention, rather than each layer computing and storing its own. This design means the model behaves externally like an ordinary autoregressive decoder while internally needing to cache key-value pairs only once, cutting the memory complexity of caching from being proportional to the number of layers down to being roughly independent of it. A further structural consequence is that, because the cross-decoder depends only on the finished output of the self-decoder, the prefill computation for the cross-decoder layers can be skipped or exited early without altering the final generated output, which directly lowers the computational cost of processing long inputs. For the self-decoder's efficient attention component, the authors propose gated retention, which extends retention with a data-dependent gating mechanism and can be computed equivalently in parallel, recurrent, or chunkwise-recurrent form, allowing efficient training while still supporting constant-memory inference. Together, the two-part architecture and the gated retention mechanism are designed to preserve the global modeling capacity associated with full attention while fundamentally changing the memory and computation scaling behavior of long-context inference.

title: Differential Transformer
author: Tianzhu Ye et al
topic: attention noise, differential attention, softmax attention
description: This paper addresses a specific failure mode of standard Transformers: the softmax attention mechanism tends to spread non-trivial weight across irrelevant parts of the context, which the authors call attention noise, and this drowns out signal from the truly relevant tokens even when they are present in context. To fix this, the authors propose Differential Transformer, which computes two separate softmax attention maps over split query and key vectors and takes their difference, scaled by a learnable parameter, as the actual attention score, rather than using a single softmax map as in standard attention. The intuition, borrowed from differential amplifiers and noise-canceling headphones in electrical engineering, is that if the noise component is common to both softmax maps, subtracting one from the other cancels it out while preserving and amplifying the genuine signal, since the two maps are not required to agree on which tokens are relevant. The learnable scalar controlling the subtraction is reparameterized as a difference of two exponentials of learned vector dot products, initialized in a layer-dependent way, which helps synchronize learning dynamics across the two attention branches. To keep training stable and compatible with existing Transformer recipes, the architecture applies headwise normalization before concatenating heads, and the authors show analytically that the gradient flow through the differential attention mechanism has the same magnitude structure as ordinary softmax attention, so hyperparameters tuned for standard Transformers transfer without instability. Because differential attention is expressed as a combination of two ordinary softmax attention operations, it can be implemented directly on top of existing efficient attention kernels such as FlashAttention, so the architectural change requires no fundamentally new low-level primitives.

title: Retentive Network: A Successor to Transformer for Large Language Models
author: Yutao Sun et al
topic: long-context attention, recurrent networks, state-space models
description: This paper addresses the "impossible triangle" facing sequence model architectures for large language models: Transformers offer strong training parallelism and performance but suffer from O(N) per-step inference cost and memory-bound key-value caching, while prior alternatives like linear attention, recurrent networks, and state-space models each sacrifice either modeling capacity, training parallelism, or true competitiveness with Transformers. The authors' core theoretical contribution is showing that a linear recurrence with a diagonalizable state-transition matrix can be reparameterized, via absorption into the query and key projections, into a form mathematically equivalent to attention with a complex-valued relative position encoding closely related to xPos, meaning the same underlying computation can be expressed either recurrently or in parallel. Building on this equivalence, they introduce the retention mechanism, which replaces the softmax attention score with a content-aware query-key product modulated by a fixed exponential decay term, thereby removing the nonlinearity that normally prevents attention from being rewritten as a recurrence. Because retention admits three mathematically equivalent formulations, a fully parallel form for efficient GPU training, a step-by-step recurrent form with constant per-token memory and compute for inference, and a chunkwise recurrent form that processes tokens in parallel within local chunks while passing a compressed summary state across chunks, it can achieve linear-complexity long-sequence handling without giving up either training efficiency or cheap decoding. A multi-scale extension assigns each attention head its own fixed decay rate, letting different heads retain information over different effective time horizons, and adds a gating nonlinearity along with group normalization to restore representational richness lost by dropping softmax. Collectively, this reframes the recurrence-versus-attention divide as a single mechanism with multiple equivalent computational views, offering a principled route to an architecture that need not trade off parallel trainability against efficient constant-cost inference.

title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression
author: DeepSeek-AI
topic: long-context attention, causal encoder-decoder, compressed sparse attention, hierarchical sparse indexer, fp4 quantization, swabounded replay, single-pass mHC, engram conditional memory, controllable reasoning effort
description: This paper presents DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model built to address a shift in the cost bottleneck for long-horizon agentic workloads: as sparse attention has already reduced compute for long sequences, the dominant constraints have become KV cache storage in HBM, persistent cache storage on SSD or host memory, and the bandwidth needed to move that cache around. The core architectural idea is a Causal Encoder-Decoder design, inspired by YoCo, where the upper half of the transformer layers derive their global key-value states directly from the hidden states of the final encoder layer rather than recomputing them layer by layer, which nearly halves prefill computation since most of the network no longer needs a full forward pass over cached prompt tokens. To shrink the cache itself, the model introduces Compressed Sparse Attention 2, which generalizes prior sparse-attention work by jointly exploiting three previously separate compression axes (entry size, sequence-length compression, and cross-layer reuse): layers are statically assigned to Full, Reindex, or Reuse modes that respectively compute fresh global KV and indices, reuse shared KV and keys while recomputing a new sparse selection, or reuse both the KV and the selection outright, decoupling cache sharing from index reuse in a way earlier methods did not. A companion Hierarchical Sparse Indexer further reduces indexing cost in the decoder by having an initial full-context indexing pass build a shared candidate pool that subsequent reindexing layers search over, turning the per-query indexing cost from linear in context length to effectively constant. On the precision and deployment side, the paper extends quantization-aware training to represent the main KV cache in FP4 using an MXFP4-based format with a theoretically justified dynamic range, and introduces SWA Bounded Replay, a storage-computation tradeoff that avoids persisting sliding-window KV states by cheaply reconstructing them through replaying only a bounded number of recent tokens rather than a full multi-layer forward pass. Together with secondary architectural refinements such as Single-Pass mHC for reducing activation memory traffic, an Engram conditional memory module, and a controllable reasoning-effort mechanism using an exponentially decaying token penalty motivated by a marginal-utility argument, these contributions constitute a coherent, jointly optimized approach to compressing KV cache footprint across the architecture, numerical precision, and serving-system layers simultaneously.

title: DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence
author: DeepSeek-AI
topic: long-context attention, hybrid attention, compressed sparse attention, heavily compressed attention, manifold-constrained hyper-connections, muon optimizer, expert parallelism, on-policy distillation
description: The paper addresses the fundamental problem that vanilla attention's quadratic computational complexity creates a prohibitive bottleneck for scaling to ultra-long contexts, which limits both test-time reasoning scaling and emerging long-horizon agentic and cross-document tasks. To solve this, the authors introduce a hybrid attention architecture combining Compressed Sparse Attention, which compresses key-value caches along the sequence dimension before applying sparse attention over the compressed entries, with Heavily Compressed Attention, which applies even more aggressive compression while retaining dense attention, allowing the two mechanisms to trade off fine-grained and coarse-grained context modeling. A second contribution, Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections, addresses the numerical instability that arises when scaling hyper-connections (an expanded, multi-stream generalization of residual connections) across many layers; the fix constrains the residual mixing matrix to the Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices via a Sinkhorn-Knopp projection, which bounds its spectral norm and keeps the mapping non-expansive and stable under deep composition. The paper also adopts the Muon optimizer, using a hybrid Newton-Schulz orthogonalization schedule to improve convergence speed and training stability, and combines it with architectural choices such as query/key-value normalization that jointly obviate the need for auxiliary logit-clipping tricks. Beyond the architecture, the work presents a suite of systems-level innovations, including fine-grained overlap of communication and computation in expert parallelism, batch-invariant and deterministic kernels for reproducibility, a heterogeneous key-value cache layout tailored to the hybrid attention scheme, and a two-stage post-training pipeline that trains domain specialists before consolidating them into a single model via full-vocabulary on-policy distillation. Collectively, the contribution is a co-designed set of architectural, optimization, and systems techniques whose theoretical rationale is to decouple accuracy-preserving computation (dense, fine-grained attention and expressive residual streams) from cost, so that context length can scale toward one million tokens without a proportional blow-up in inference compute or memory.

title: HoPE: A Novel Positional Encoding Without Long-Term Decay for Enhanced Context Awareness and Extrapolation
author: Yuhan Chen et al
topic: rope, positional encoding, attention normalization, long-context attention
description: The paper argues that global long-term attention decay is unnecessary for modern language models, since learned attention patterns tend to combine local decay with globally U-shaped behavior rather than monotonically decreasing with distance. Through decomposition of RoPE attention into frequency-specific components, it identifies activated low-frequency components as the primary source of the U-shaped pattern and as a constraint on optimization and length extrapolation. These activated components become out-of-distribution when positions extend beyond the training context, producing anomalous first-layer attention logits that propagate through subsequent layers. The paper also finds that the lowest-frequency RoPE components tend toward nearly constant patterns, suggesting that their representational capacity is better suited to semantic information than positional encoding. HoPE addresses these issues by replacing the activated and top low-frequency RoPE components with position-independent components while retaining the higher-frequency rotary components, yielding an attention formulation that removes the imposed global decay while preserving relative positional information. The resulting mechanism reduces frequency-induced constraints and extrapolation distribution shifts, allowing positional and semantic representation subspaces to be used more flexibly.

title: Rope to Nope and Back Again: A New Hybrid Attention Strategy
author: Bowen Yang et al
topic: rope, positional encoding, attention normalization, long-context attention
description: The paper analyzes RoPE, NoPE, and QK-Norm to characterize how positional encoding and attention normalization shape long-context attention behavior. It finds that NoPE naturally promotes similarity-based long-range retrieval, while RoPE provides a strong recency bias and local-context aggregation, whereas QK-Norm flattens attention logits and weakens the attention-sink behavior. The proposed RNoPE architecture interleaves NoPE and RoPE layers, leading to an emergent division of labor in which NoPE layers specialize in global retrieval and RoPE layers specialize in local information processing. The work further shows that increasing RoPE’s θ in this hybrid architecture can interfere with NoPE retrieval by making RoPE attention less localized, motivating explicit restriction of RoPE layers to a sliding attention window. RNoPE-SWA therefore removes QK-Norm, gives full attention to NoPE layers, and applies sliding-window attention to RoPE layers, with a 1:3 full-attention-to-windowed-layer interleaving chosen to balance the two roles. This design reduces the quadratic attention workload for most layers to O(SL), where S is the local window size, while preserving full-context retrieval through the NoPE layers and substantially reducing training and inference memory and computation.

title: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalizeation in Transformers
author: Amirhossein Kazemnejad et al
topic: nope, positional encoding, length generalization
description: This work systematically studies how positional encoding affects length generalization in decoder-only Transformers, comparing absolute, relative, rotary, ALiBi, and no positional encoding mechanisms. Its central technical finding is that causal self-attention can recover positional structure even without explicit positional encodings, making explicit position representations unnecessary for the architecture. Theoretically, the authors show that a NoPE Transformer can construct absolute positional information in its first layer and subsequently use that representation to implement relative positional attention in later layers. This establishes that positional information can emerge internally through the interaction of causal masking, self-attention, and learned feed-forward transformations rather than being injected into token representations. To characterize the mechanism learned during optimization, the work introduces an attention-pattern distance based on Jensen-Shannon divergence and finds that NoPE attention structurally resembles T5-style relative positional attention across layers. The analysis further shows that positional encoding determines the spatial structure of attention, with NoPE and relative bias supporting both short- and long-range dependencies while ALiBi imposes recency bias, providing a mechanistic explanation for their differing extrapolation behavior.

title: LoLCATs: On Low-Rank Linearization of Large Language Models
author: Michael Zhang et al
topic: linear attention, softmax, low-rank adaptation, LoRA
description: LoLCATs frames linearizing an LLM as a two-step problem: first train subquadratic attention analogs to imitate the model's existing softmax attentions ("attention transfer"), then swap the attentions in and correct residual approximation error with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) on the query, key, value, and output projections, leaving all other weights frozen. Attention transfer is cast as a feature map learning problem, where learnable maps phi_q and phi_k are inserted after the existing query and key projections and trained to minimize the mean squared error between linear and softmax attention outputs per head and layer, with the original attention outputs teacher-forced into subsequent layers so errors do not propagate; supervising on outputs rather than on the n-by-n attention weights, as prior distillation work did, reduces memory from quadratic to linear in sequence length and lets both branches use FlashAttention-style or recurrent kernels. Because the maps are applied after rotary embeddings, the parameterization preserves the kernel interpretation in which phi_q(q)^T phi_k(k) directly approximates exp(q^T k / sqrt(d)). To handle the low-entropy, "spiky" attention distributions that pure linear attention approximates poorly, the paper generalizes the analog to a hybrid layer that computes exact softmax attention over a short sliding window of recent tokens and linear attention over everything before it, combined through a learnable mixing term and a log-sum-exp stabilizing constant, which keeps generation linear in time and constant in memory while lowering matching error. Finally, since jointly optimizing one MSE objective over all layers concentrates error in later layers and fails outright at very large depth, training is partitioned into independent blocks of b layers whose inputs can be precomputed from the original Transformer, with b chosen via a simple cost model trading per-block quality against GPU memory, parallel training time, and the disk cost of storing precomputed hidden states.

title: The Hedgehog and the Porcupine: Expressive Linear Attentions with Softmax Mimicry
author: Michael Zhang et al
topic: linear attention, softmax mimicry
description: Hedgehog addresses the quality gap between linear attention and standard softmax attention by first diagnosing what prior linear attentions lack: low-entropy or "spiky" attention weight distributions that selectively concentrate on relevant tokens, and monotonicity of attention weights with respect to query-key dot products, whose absence can produce conflicting gradients when swapping attention layers into an existing model. As an initial check on this diagnosis, the authors show that a second-degree Taylor approximation of the exponential recovers both properties in the bounded dot-product regimes encountered in practice, but its feature map expands a d-dimensional vector to roughly d-squared dimensions, giving cubic-in-head-dimension cost that erases the practical efficiency gains. The core contribution is to replace a fixed, hand-designed kernel with a learned one: a single-layer MLP applied to queries and keys, using an element-wise exponential activation to induce spikiness, mapping from d dimensions back to d and thus preserving the O(nd^2) complexity of earlier linear attentions. This feature map is trained by softmax mimicry, minimizing a cross-entropy distillation loss between the normalized linear attention weights and the weights the softmax attention would have assigned, with a separate MLP learned per head and per layer. The resulting method supports three deployment regimes with the same machinery: training from scratch by initializing the MLPs near identity and learning end-to-end, finetuned-conversion by distilling attention weights and then finetuning on the original task, and pretrained-conversion of large models, where the distilled linear attention can be adapted with low-rank updates rather than full retraining.

title: Retrofitting Linear Attention into Diffusion Language Models
author: Jinha Kim et al
topic: dlm, linear attention, diffusion language models
description: This work introduces block-hybrid attention, which retains exact bidirectional softmax attention among tokens inside the active denoising block of a block-diffusion language model while summarizing all previously committed blocks with Hedgehog linear attention, using a learned positive feature map applied per query head to build two fixed-size recurrent states that are updated once each block is committed. The two branches are merged through a shared denominator with a learned per-head scalar gate, so the attention mass is balanced between the active block and the committed context rather than each branch being normalized independently, and the only new parameters per linearized layer are the feature-map matrices and the gates. To retrofit this into an existing pretrained diffusion model without training from scratch, the authors adapt the two-stage LoLCATs recipe to the diffusion setting: Stage 1 freezes the backbone and trains only the feature maps and gates to match each replaced softmax layer's pre-projection output under an MSE attention-transfer loss with cross-layer teacher forcing, so each layer's error is isolated, and Stage 2 freezes both the backbone and the hybrid parameters while training LoRA adapters on the attention and MLP projections under the standard masked-token diffusion objective to correct residual cross-layer mismatch. Corruption during retrofitting is applied only to assistant-response tokens, leaving prompt tokens unmasked to match the conditional-generation interface used at inference. For serving, the block-hybrid module is implemented as a single fused Triton kernel in SGLang that computes the within-block softmax branch, the linear state readout, the gated merge, and the state update in one launch without writing intermediates to HBM, with the recurrent state stored per query head alongside the existing paged KV cache so it reuses the same slot allocator and continuous-batching scheduler, giving per-request memory and per-pass cost for linearized layers that are constant in sequence length.

title: Reducing Pretraining-Generation Mismatch in Diffusion Language Models
author: Xiaocheng Lu et al
topic: dlm, diffusion language models
description: This work identifies a pretraining-generation mismatch in diffusion language models: native dLLM pretraining corrupts tokens across the whole sequence, including the prompt, even though prompt-continuation evaluation always supplies a clean prefix. The authors propose Prefix-Conditioned Diffusion (PCD), a continued-pretraining objective that splits each sequence at a sampled latent boundary, supervises the clean prefix with a standard autoregressive next-token loss, and applies no-shift masked diffusion reconstruction to the corrupted suffix conditioned on that clean prefix, implemented purely by changing the attention mask, corruption mask, and label construction without any new decoder, verifier, or inference mode. PCD is positioned as a stable-phase intervention inside a Warmup-Stable-Decay AR-to-diffusion conversion pipeline, leaving the warmup and decay stages intact, and it instantiates naturally with block diffusion while also applying to full-sequence diffusion. A variational analysis formalizes the benefit, showing that replacing the corrupted prefix with the clean prefix removes a non-negative context-shift term equal to the conditional mutual information between the suffix and the clean prefix given the corrupted prefix. The method further disentangles two degrees of freedom, intra-sample mixing of the AR-prefix and MDM-suffix losses within one sequence and inter-sample Bernoulli mixing of PCD and native diffusion examples across a minibatch, allowing the local clean-prefix alignment signal to be isolated from batch-level objective regularization.

title: Glancing Transformer for Non-Autoregressive Neural Machine Translation
author: Lihua Qian et al
topic: non-autoregressive generation, machine translation, curriculum learning
description: Glancing Transformer (GLAT) addresses the core weakness of fully non-autoregressive translation: independently predicting every target token prevents the decoder from learning strong dependencies between target words, while iterative masked prediction restores those dependencies only by sacrificing the speed advantage of single-pass decoding.
