The key contribution is the Glancing Language Model (GLM), which turns dependency learning into a training-time curriculum: the model first makes a fully parallel prediction, measures how far that prediction is from the reference, then exposes a subset of correct reference tokens to a second parallel decoding pass and trains the model to predict the remaining tokens conditioned on those exposed words. Implementation-wise, the first decoder pass produces predictions Ŷ from encoder-derived representations H, the Hamming distance d(Y, Ŷ) determines the number of reference tokens to reveal as S = λd(Y, Ŷ), and S reference positions are randomly selected; their ground-truth word embeddings then replace the corresponding encoder-derived decoder inputs to form H′, which is fed through the decoder a second time and optimized using cross-entropy on the remaining, unrevealed target tokens. The adaptive sampling is what creates the curriculum: when the model is poor, its prediction error is large, so many correct reference tokens are supplied and the model solves an easier fragment-completion problem; as training improves, the error decreases and fewer reference tokens are supplied, progressively forcing the decoder to generate larger portions of the sequence independently until it can generate the complete sequence without any reference tokens. A second important implementation choice is that GLAT does not insert [MASK] tokens at the sampled positions; instead, it replaces the corresponding decoder inputs with the actual target word embeddings while retaining the encoder-derived representations elsewhere, allowing the sampled words to interact naturally with both source information and the other decoder representations.

title: Aligned Cross Entropy for Non-Autoregressive Machine Translation
author: Marjan Ghazvininejad et al
topic: non-autoregressive generation, machine translation, loss functions
description: Aligned Cross Entropy (AXE) addresses a fundamental problem in non-autoregressive generation: standard cross-entropy assumes that the token at position i must match the target token at exactly position i, so a small positional shift causes many otherwise-correct predictions to receive large penalties. The core contribution is to replace position-by-position cross entropy with a loss that searches for the best monotonic alignment between the target token sequence and the model's sequence of probability distributions, thereby emphasizing lexical correctness and relative order rather than exact absolute positions. Implementation-wise, AXE constructs an (n+1)×(m+1) dynamic-programming matrix where each cell stores the minimum loss for aligning prefixes of the target and prediction sequences, and each cell chooses among three operations: align a target with a prediction, skip a prediction by treating it as a blank ε token, or skip a target by effectively reusing the current prediction; the δ parameter controls how costly target skipping is. Although the underlying dynamic program is O(nm), they implement it efficiently on GPUs by computing all cells on the same anti-diagonal simultaneously, reducing the sequential depth to O(n+m), so the extra loss computation is relatively small compared with the Transformer's forward and backward passes. They then plug AXE directly into conditional masked language model training without modifying the Transformer architecture or parallel argmax decoding, and adapt the model to produce blank tokens that can absorb redundant predictions; during training they find it is preferable to expose some target tokens while focusing the loss on masked tokens, effectively making the optimization easier while keeping the learning signal concentrated on the actual prediction task. The deeper contribution is that AXE changes what the model is encouraged to learn: instead of hedging probability across neighboring positions because it fears being slightly misaligned, the model can confidently predict a token at one position while the alignment procedure accounts for small shifts, producing sharper positional predictions and substantially reducing the inconsistent repetitions associated with multimodal non-autoregressive generation.

title: Semi-Autoregressive Training Improves Mask-Predict Decoding
author: Marjan Ghazvininejad et al
topic: masked language models, parallel decoding, non-autoregressive generation
description: SMART fixes a key train–test mismatch in Mask-Predict: the original CMLM is trained with correct ground-truth tokens as context, whereas at inference it must condition on its own imperfect predictions, so the model is never explicitly trained to recover from its own errors. The core contribution is Semi-Autoregressive Training (SMART), which generates training inputs using the model itself: it first masks a random subset of the gold target, runs the CMLM to produce a predicted sequence, then randomly masks a different subset of that predicted sequence and trains the model to reconstruct the original gold sequence from this noisy, prediction-derived context. This is implemented as a two-forward-pass training procedure: the first pass creates the model-generated training example, while gradients are applied only to the second pass, where cross-entropy is computed over all target tokens rather than only the masked ones because the observed tokens themselves may contain model errors that the network must learn to correct. They also modify inference so that each refinement step predicts every target position, rather than only masked positions, and replaces a token whenever the new prediction differs from the current input, making the training and inference procedures more closely aligned. An important implementation insight is that SMART deliberately samples training examples across a spectrum of difficulty: partially masking the gold sequence gives the model some reliable “seed” information, while masking more gold tokens forces it to operate increasingly on its own predictions; completely removing the gold context is too difficult, so the useful regime is learning to recover from imperfect predictions while retaining some ground-truth signal.

title: Mask-Predict: Parallel Decoding of Conditional Masked Language Models
author: Marjan Ghazvininejad et al
topic: masked language models, parallel decoding, non-autoregressive generation
description: Mask-Predict introduces conditional masked language models (CMLMs), an encoder-decoder Transformer whose decoder removes the usual causal attention mask, allowing every target position to attend to both left and right context and therefore predict masked tokens in parallel. During training, they randomly choose how many target tokens to mask, uniformly from one token up to the entire sequence, replace those positions with a MASK token, and train the model with cross-entropy only on the masked positions, forcing it to learn to reconstruct arbitrary subsets of a target sequence rather than follow a fixed left-to-right order. At inference, they first predict the entire target sequence simultaneously from a completely masked sequence, then repeatedly identify the tokens with the lowest model confidence, mask only those tokens, and regenerate them conditioned on the higher-confidence tokens; the masking ratio decreases linearly across a fixed number of iterations, so computation shifts from broad parallel generation toward increasingly targeted refinement. Because parallel generation requires knowing the target length beforehand, they add a special LENGTH token to the encoder, train it to predict the target length, and then decode several of the most likely length candidates in parallel, selecting the resulting sequence with the highest average token log-probability. The key contribution is therefore not simply parallel prediction, but an iterative error-correction mechanism: uncertain predictions are explicitly revisited while confident predictions become fixed context, which lets the model progressively resolve ambiguities and mitigate the multimodality and repetition problems that make one-shot non-autoregressive generation unreliable.

title: Extreme Compression of Large Language Models via Additive Quantization
author: Vage Egiazarian et al
topic: quantization, llm, post-training quantization, outliers
description: This paper introduces AQLM (Additive Quantization for Language Models), which adapts a technique from nearest-neighbor search called Additive Quantization to compress LLM weights down to extremely low bit-widths, around 2 to 3 bits per parameter, while preserving much more accuracy than prior methods like GPTQ or QuIP. The core idea is to represent each group of weights not as a single rounded value, but as a sum of vectors chosen from several learned codebooks, so each weight group is reconstructed by picking one code from each of multiple codebooks and adding them together, rather than concatenating them as in simpler product quantization schemes. Critically, the codebooks and codes are optimized not to minimize error on the raw weights themselves, but to minimize the error in the layer's actual output given real calibration input data, which makes the compression input-aware rather than purely weight-aware. The optimization proceeds in three phases: codes are initialized using residual K-means clustering, then codes are refined via a beam search formulated as MAP inference over a Markov Random Field with precomputed pairwise and unary potentials, and codebooks plus per-unit scales are updated using Adam-based gradient descent, with these two steps alternating until convergence. A third phase then fine-tunes the codebooks and non-quantized parameters (such as normalization layers) jointly across an entire transformer block, using calibration data to correct for compounding errors between multiple quantized layers, which meaningfully boosts accuracy since prior work mostly optimized each layer in isolation. Beyond the algorithm itself, the authors contribute practical GPU and CPU kernels that make AQLM efficient at inference time, achieving speeds comparable to or exceeding full-precision baselines despite the added complexity of decoding additive codes, while cutting memory footprint substantially, and they show the resulting compressed models are the first to achieve Pareto-optimal accuracy-versus-size tradeoffs below three bits per parameter.

title: SpQR: A Sparse-Quantized Representation for Near-Lossless LLM Weight Compression
author: Tim Dettmers et al
topic: quantization, llm, post-training quantization, outliers
description: SpQR is a post-training quantization method that compresses LLM weights to 3-4 bits per parameter while staying near-lossless relative to the 16-bit model, addressing the fact that standard low-bit quantization causes significant accuracy loss, especially in smaller models. The key insight driving the method is a sensitivity analysis showing that quantization error is not randomly distributed across weight matrices but concentrated in structured patterns, such as specific attention heads, rotary embedding dimensions, and row or column outliers, alongside scattered unstructured outliers. Building on this, SpQR isolates the small fraction of highly sensitive weights (identified via a Hessian-based sensitivity criterion adapted from the Optimal Brain Surgeon framework and computed efficiently during a GPTQ-style layer-wise quantization pass) and stores them separately in 16-bit precision using a compressed-sparse-row format, while the remaining bulk of weights are quantized to low bitwidth. To make the low-bit quantization itself more accurate, the method uses very small quantization groups so that scale and zero-point statistics can adapt to local weight behavior, and then addresses the resulting metadata overhead by recursively quantizing those group-level statistics themselves in a second level of quantization. The full pipeline works by first detecting outliers within each group, then fitting quantization statistics on the remaining non-outlier weights, quantizing them, and propagating the resulting error to unquantized weights using the inverse Hessian, following the same error-compensation logic as GPTQ. To make this representation practical, the authors also built a custom GPU inference kernel that loads outlier and quantized weight data into shared memory and performs load-balanced sparse-dense matrix multiplication, achieving faster token generation than a 16-bit baseline despite the added complexity of handling outliers, while reducing memory footprint substantially.

title: Hogwild! Inference: Parallel LLM Generation via Concurrent Attention
author: Gleb Rodionov et al
topic: inference, parallelism, kv cache, rotary position embeddings
description: Hogwild! Inference lets multiple instances of the same LLM generate text in parallel while sharing a single, concurrently-updated Key-Value cache, so each worker can see the others' tokens as they're produced rather than following a pre-defined division of labor. The core technical trick is handling Rotary Position Embeddings: since the same cached tokens appear at different relative positions for different workers, the authors avoid expensive re-encoding by instead rotating the current query at each step to an equivalent angle for each cache block, exploiting the fact that attention scores only depend on the relative rotation between query and key. This lets them reuse existing KV representations directly, with only a single query rotation per worker per step rather than re-rotating potentially huge amounts of cached history. To keep workers meaningfully synchronized over long generations, they structure the cache like a group chat: text is split into paragraph-sized "steps," and when a worker finishes a step its cache is appended to a shared history block, while other workers can still see that worker's current, unfinished step as it's being written. Each worker's view is thus composed of a common cache (system prompt and finished history), blocks from other workers' in-progress steps, and its own current step. Collaboration itself is achieved purely through prompting rather than fine-tuning: a system prompt explains the shared-cache setup and encourages cooperation, and periodically a worker is asked whether it might be doing redundant work, nudging it to notice and correct overlap with other workers. The authors implement this efficiently with custom GPU kernels built on FlashAttention/Paged-Attention-style batching, demonstrating that inference throughput scales favorably as more workers are added, showing the method's viability beyond a proof of concept.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Promise and Performance for Microscaling FP4 Quantization
author: Vage Egiazarian et al
topic: ptq, quantization, fp4, mxfp4, nvfp4
description: This paper studies MXFP4 and NVFP4, two hardware-accelerated 4-bit floating-point formats for quantizing LLM weights and activations, and finds that naive application of state-of-the-art quantization methods fails to realize their promised accuracy gains: NVFP4's small group size makes Hadamard rotation-based outlier mitigation counterproductive, while MXFP4's power-of-two-only scale representation introduces large inherent quantization error. Their core contribution, Micro-Rotated-GPTQ (MR-GPTQ), adapts the classic GPTQ algorithm specifically to these formats by combining three ingredients: block-wise Hadamard rotations applied to both weights and activations to reshape heavy-tailed distributions into more quantization-friendly normal-like distributions, MSE-optimized scale search for the quantization grids rather than simple absmax scaling, and a "static" version of activation reordering that reorders columns before scale computation (rather than dynamically at runtime), preserving GPTQ's accuracy benefits without incurring inference-time overhead. To make the rotation step practical, they fuse the weight-side rotation directly into the stored weights ahead of time, so only the activation-side rotation needs to happen online during inference, and they built QuTLASS, a set of custom GPU kernels for NVIDIA Blackwell hardware that perform this online rotation, quantization, and scale computation as a single fused operation with minimal added latency. The GPTQ error-correction step is essentially orthogonal to the rotation and grid design choices, letting error introduced by aggressive quantization in one part of a weight matrix be compensated for by adjustments elsewhere, and MR-GPTQ shows this combines well with rotation-normalized distributions for both formats. Empirically, MR-GPTQ substantially closes the accuracy gap between MXFP4 and NVFP4 relative to naive quantization approaches, while NVFP4 alone tends to already perform reasonably with simpler methods since its finer per-group scale representation and smaller group size preserve outliers better without needing rotation. On the systems side, their kernels achieve inference throughput close to the theoretical hardware ceiling for both formats, demonstrating that the added computational cost of rotation and scale-fitting can be made nearly free in practice, making format-specialized quantization a viable path to real speedups over half-precision inference rather than just a theoretical one.

title: DuQuant: Distributing Outliers via Dual Transformation Makes Stronger Quantized LLMs
author: Haokun Lin et al
topic: llm, quantization, outliers, dual transformation
description: DuQuant proposes a post-training quantization method that improves low-bit weight-activation quantization by explicitly handling two types of activation outliers: persistent normal outliers that appear across many tokens and rare but extremely large massive outliers that existing methods such as SmoothQuant fail to eliminate effectively. The method first applies standard activation-weight smoothing, then constructs a block-diagonal orthogonal rotation matrix using a greedy search that repeatedly identifies the most extreme activation dimensions and builds rotations that redistribute those large values across neighboring channels while preserving the exact linear transformation by applying the inverse rotation to the weights. Because independent block-wise rotations can leave some blocks much harder to quantize than others, DuQuant introduces a zigzag permutation that globally reorders channels so that high- and low-magnitude activation channels are evenly distributed across blocks before applying a second block-wise rotation, allowing outliers to be further diffused within each balanced block. The entire transformation is represented as a single invertible matrix composed of smoothing, rotation, permutation, and another rotation, with the corresponding inverse fused into the weight matrix offline, producing quantization-friendly activations and weights without changing the model's computation or requiring expensive reconstruction algorithms such as GPTQ. The paper also provides theoretical analysis showing that the greedy rotations monotonically reduce the largest activation magnitudes within each block while the zigzag permutation bounds variance between blocks, explaining why the combined transformations improve quantization behavior. The main contribution is a simple and efficient dual-transformation pipeline that jointly redistributes activation and weight outliers, introduces a novel zigzag permutation strategy for balancing block difficulty, eliminates the need for complex weight optimization during quantization, and enables stronger low-bit LLM quantization through purely offline linear transformations.

title: WUSH: Near-Optimal Adaptive Transforms for LLM Quantization
author: Jiale Chen et al
topic: llm, quantization, adaptive transforms
description: WUSH introduces a closed-form, data-aware blockwise transform for large language model weight-activation quantization, addressing the limitation of fixed transforms such as Hadamard rotations that cannot adapt to the statistics of individual weight and activation blocks. The method first computes blockwise second-moment matrices for weights and calibration activations, performs Cholesky decompositions followed by an SVD of their cross-covariance, and analytically constructs paired transforms consisting of a Hadamard matrix, singular-value scaling, and data-dependent whitening factors, yielding mutually inverse transforms for weights and activations that jointly minimize quantization error. Unlike prior learned transforms that require iterative optimization on calibration data, WUSH derives its transforms directly in closed form, can be integrated into both RTN and GPTQ by reusing the activation Hessian already computed during GPTQ calibration, and interleaves transform recomputation with GPTQ's blockwise weight updates to preserve second-order accuracy. The authors provide theoretical proofs that this construction is optimal for floating-point block quantizers and asymptotically near-optimal for integer block quantizers by analyzing stochastic quantization error models, showing that the adaptive non-orthogonal scaling complements the Hadamard mixing to reduce the impact of outliers beyond what any orthogonal transform can achieve. To make the approach practical, they implement a fused GPU kernel that applies the per-block transforms and activation quantization together using a GEMM-based design, storing one transform per block while exploiting cache locality so runtime overhead remains nearly identical to optimized Hadamard implementations. Overall, the paper's main contribution is demonstrating that quantization-optimal transforms need not be learned through optimization but can instead be derived analytically from second-order statistics, providing both theoretical guarantees and an efficient implementation that consistently reduces quantization error and improves low-bit quantized model quality across floating-point and integer formats.

title: GPTailor: Large Language Model Pruning Through Layer Cutting and Stitching
author: Guinan Su et al
topic: llm, pruning, structured pruning, layer stitching
description: GPTailor proposes a new approach to structured LLM pruning by treating compression as the problem of constructing a smaller model from a pool of related fine-tuned variants rather than pruning a single checkpoint in isolation. Their method defines a search space over three operations—layer removal, layer selection from different fine-tuned models, and layer merging using configurable merge algorithms such as task arithmetic—and formulates the entire design process as a constrained zero-order optimization problem that searches for the best architecture under a target pruning ratio. To evaluate candidate architectures, they optimize a multi-objective function over several calibration tasks using ParEGO scalarization, allowing the search to preserve diverse capabilities instead of overfitting to a single metric, while SMAC performs efficient multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization by first evaluating candidates on small calibration subsets before allocating larger evaluation budgets only to promising configurations. The resulting compressed model is assembled by stitching together layers originating from different specialized fine-tuned models, optionally merging multiple candidate layers into a single layer, enabling task-specific knowledge from different variants to be consolidated without any additional post-training or recovery finetuning. Through extensive ablations, the authors show that the combination of cross-model layer stitching, learned layer merging, and multi-objective search is substantially more effective than pruning alone, naive layer replacement, within-model layer folding, or perplexity-guided optimization, indicating that preserving complementary knowledge across model variants is the key factor behind the gains. Overall, the paper's main contribution is reframing structured pruning as an automated architecture search over a family of related models, demonstrating that intelligently cutting and stitching layers from specialized fine-tuned checkpoints can produce significantly smaller models that retain most of the original model's capabilities while avoiding expensive retraining.

title: Upcycling Large Language Models into Mixture of Experts
author: Ethan He et al
topic: mixture of experts, upcycling, large language models
description: The paper presents a practical recipe for converting pretrained dense transformer language models into sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models through upcycling, demonstrating that expanding model capacity from an existing checkpoint is more effective than simply continuing dense training under the same compute budget. The implementation duplicates each dense MLP into multiple experts while replacing every feed-forward layer with an MoE layer, randomly initializes a router, and introduces a novel virtual group initialization for fine-grained MoEs that first shards each dense MLP along its hidden dimension, replicates every shard into multiple experts, and initializes router weights so that each token initially selects exactly one replica from every shard, preserving the dense network's functional behavior at the start of training. To compensate for the reduced activation magnitude introduced by routing probabilities and expert sharding, the authors derive and apply an analytical weight scaling rule that rescales both input and output projection matrices of every expert before training, avoiding architectural changes while maintaining stable activation scales and improving convergence for both coarse- and fine-grained MoEs. Through extensive ablations, they further show that softmax-then-topK routing consistently surpasses topK-then-softmax once proper weight scaling is applied because it preserves richer routing information, and they identify upcycling-specific optimization practices including resetting the learning rate to a higher value, using larger batch sizes, and carefully tuning load-balancing loss while finding that additional router regularization provides little benefit. The study also analyzes architectural tradeoffs by varying expert granularity, routing topK, shared experts, and expert diversification strategies, concluding that finer-grained experts and larger routing fan-out can improve optimization but exhibit diminishing returns and require careful initialization to avoid poor convergence. Overall, the paper's main contribution is a complete engineering recipe for scalable MoE upcycling—including virtual group initialization, analytical weight scaling, routing recommendations, and optimized training hyperparameters—that enables pretrained dense models to be reliably transformed into larger sparse MoE models without training from scratch.

title: Why Muon Outperforms Adam: A Curvature Perspective
author: Shuche Wang et al
topic: muon, adam, optimization, curvature, hessian
description: This paper explains Muon’s optimization advantage over Adam through a curvature-based analysis rather than optimizer heuristics, showing that Muon consistently achieves larger one-step loss reductions because its updates incur a smaller second-order curvature penalty despite having similar first-order gradient alignment. The authors analyze optimization using a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, decomposing each update into a gradient-alignment term and a Hessian-based curvature penalty, then further separating the curvature penalty into update magnitude and Normalized Directional Sharpness (NDS), a metric measuring the curvature encountered along the update direction independent of its scale. They show that Muon’s implementation, which forms a momentum matrix, spectrally normalizes it by replacing all nonzero singular values with one using an orthogonalized update (approximated efficiently via Newton–Schulz iterations rather than exact SVD), produces update directions with substantially lower NDS than Adam while maintaining comparable update norms, demonstrating that its advantage comes from choosing flatter directions instead of taking smaller steps. The paper further investigates why this occurs by showing that increasing dataset imbalance amplifies Muon’s NDS advantage and by decomposing Hessian curvature into within-layer and cross-layer components, revealing that Muon increasingly concentrates its advantage in reduced within-layer curvature as training progresses. To explain these observations theoretically, the authors construct a structured quadratic optimization model with heterogeneous curvature, low-rank Kronecker Hessian structure, and gradient alignment toward sharp directions, proving that Muon’s spectral normalization distributes update energy more evenly across curvature modes, whereas gradient descent and Adam concentrate updates in sharper directions, increasing directional sharpness. Overall, the paper’s main contribution is identifying reduced normalized directional sharpness as the fundamental mechanism behind Muon’s superior optimization behavior, connecting its matrix orthogonalization procedure directly to lower curvature costs and providing both empirical and theoretical evidence that this geometric property explains its improved training efficiency.

title: Understanding Adam Requires Better Rotation Dependent Assumptions
author: Tianyue H. Zhang et al
topic: adam, optimization, rotation invariance
description: The paper investigates why Adam consistently outperforms SGD by studying its sensitivity to rotations of the parameter space, arguing that Adam's optimization behavior fundamentally depends on the choice of coordinate basis rather than being rotation-invariant. To evaluate this, the authors implement a training procedure that leaves model weights in the original parameterization but rotates gradients into an alternative basis before applying Adam, then rotates the resulting parameter update back into the original space, allowing standard forward and backward passes while isolating the optimizer's behavior under different coordinate systems. They systematically compare random rotations at different granularities and introduce a structured SVD-based rotation that decomposes each layer's gradient into singular vectors and singular values, periodically recomputes this basis, performs Adam updates in the rotated coordinates, and transforms the updates back, showing that carefully chosen rotations can improve optimization whereas arbitrary rotations often reduce Adam's effectiveness. The authors further analyze why this occurs by examining how rotations affect Adam's second-moment statistics, Hessian structure, gradient bounds, and update geometry, finding that commonly assumed theoretical explanations such as L∞ gradient bounds and block-diagonal Hessians do not consistently predict Adam's empirical behavior across different bases. Instead, they observe that the degree of orthogonality of each layer's update matrix, measured through the variation of its singular values, closely tracks optimization quality and naturally connects Adam's behavior to recent orthogonal update methods such as Muon and SOAP. The main contribution is demonstrating that Adam's success is inherently basis-dependent, introducing a practical framework for studying optimization under arbitrary parameter-space rotations, identifying structured rotations that enhance optimization, and proposing update orthogonality as a more promising theoretical principle for explaining and designing adaptive optimizers.

title: Dynamic Mixture of Experts: An Auto-Tuning Approach for Efficient Transformers Models
author: Yongxin Guo et al
topic: moe, routing, dynamic allocation
description: DynMoE removes two major Mixture-of-Experts hyperparameters by allowing both the number of active experts per token (top-k) and the total number of experts to adapt automatically during training instead of being fixed beforehand. Instead of conventional top-k routing, the router computes cosine similarity between each token and learned expert embeddings, compares each similarity against a trainable threshold for that expert, independently activates every expert whose score exceeds its threshold (top-any routing), averages the outputs of the selected experts equally, and falls back to top-1 routing only when no expert is selected during inference to prevent dropped tokens. To encourage sparse but diverse routing, the method replaces standard load-balancing losses with an auxiliary objective that orthogonalizes expert representations while regularizing their norms, promoting specialization without forcing every expert to receive equal traffic. During training, the router records which experts were used and accumulates embeddings of tokens that matched no expert; if unmatched tokens appear, a new expert is added by initializing its routing vector from the normalized average embedding of those tokens, while experts that remain unused for an extended period are removed, allowing the expert pool itself to grow or shrink dynamically. This adaptive process is performed periodically rather than every iteration to reduce overhead, with configurable upper limits on the maximum number of experts to satisfy hardware constraints. Overall, the paper demonstrates that jointly learning routing thresholds and dynamically managing the expert pool eliminates expensive hyperparameter tuning while maintaining sparse computation, competitive accuracy, and revealing architectural insights such as lower layers benefiting from greater expert diversity than upper layers.

title: DA-MoE: Towards Dynamic Expert Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Models
author: Maryam Akhavan Aghdam et al
topic: moe, routing, dynamic allocation
description: DA-MoE extends a standard Transformer-based Mixture-of-Experts model by replacing the conventional fixed top-K router with a dynamic routing mechanism that assigns a different number of experts to each token based on its estimated importance, arguing that semantically important tokens should receive more computation while less informative tokens require fewer experts. Token importance is computed directly from the Transformer's final attention layer by taking, for each token, the maximum attention value within each attention head and averaging these maxima across all heads, producing a normalized importance score that is multiplied by the total number of experts and rounded up to determine the token-specific routing budget K. After determining K, the router itself remains largely unchanged: router logits are computed from a learned linear projection of the token embedding, converted to routing probabilities with a softmax, and the top-K experts are selected instead of a globally fixed top-1 or top-2 routing strategy. The implementation also preserves standard MoE capacity constraints by generating expert assignment masks, tracking each token's position within an expert, and dropping assignments that exceed expert capacity, allowing the approach to be integrated into existing Switch Transformer-style architectures with minimal architectural modifications beyond the routing logic. The key contribution is demonstrating that attention scores can serve as a simple heuristic for token importance, enabling adaptive allocation of computation across tokens without modifying the attention or expert networks themselves. Overall, the paper proposes a lightweight routing modification that dynamically varies expert usage according to attention-derived token importance, improving the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff while remaining compatible with existing sparse MoE implementations.

title: DAG-MoE: From Simple Mixture to Structural Aggregation in Mixture-of-Experts
author: Jiarui Feng et al
topic: moe, routing, dag, structural aggregation
description: DAG-MoE replaces the standard weighted-sum aggregation of selected MoE experts with a learned directed acyclic graph (DAG), arguing that structural composition increases the expressive power of an MoE layer without changing the router or the experts themselves. After the router selects the top-K experts as usual, each expert output becomes a node, and a lightweight DAG learning module iteratively learns pairwise connections by projecting expert features into a lower-dimensional space, concatenating node pairs, predicting edge gates with small MLPs, gating message passing between nodes, applying residual connections, and repeating this process for multiple iterations before summing the final node representations as the layer output. Unlike prior approaches that rely on fixed tree structures or multiple routing stages, the method performs routing only once and dynamically learns a token-dependent aggregation structure, allowing different inputs to induce different expert interaction patterns with relatively little additional computation. The authors theoretically prove that this structural aggregation is strictly more expressive than permutation-invariant weighted summation because it can distinguish different expert orderings and graph structures, and they further show that a single DAG-style MoE layer can approximate multi-step compositional reasoning, such as dynamic programming computations, through iterative message passing over the learned graph. The implementation is intentionally lightweight, using small projection layers, learned edge-gating networks, residual updates, shared parameters across iterations, zero initialization for stability, and a configurable hidden dimension independent of the model or expert size, making it easy to integrate into existing MoE architectures. Overall, the paper's main contribution is introducing structural aggregation as a new scaling axis for MoE models that complements expert count and routing improvements, demonstrating that learning how experts interact can improve model capacity more effectively than simply adding parameters or additional shared experts.

title: HALO: Hadamard-Assisted Lower Precision Optimization for LLMs
author: Saleh Ashkboos et al
topic: quantization, qat, fp4, training
description: HALO introduces a quantization-aware fine-tuning method that enables all large matrix multiplications in Transformer forward and backward passes to execute in low precision while preserving accuracy by strategically inserting Hadamard rotations to suppress activation, weight, and gradient outliers. The authors first analyze quantization sensitivity during fine-tuning and show that the forward pass is particularly vulnerable because activation outliers corrupt weight gradients, while backward error tensors contain column-wise outliers that require left-hand-side Hadamard rotations rather than the right-hand-side rotations commonly used in inference quantization. Based on this analysis, they propose two variants: HALO-1, which applies right-hand-side Hadamard transformations to weights and activations so that transformed tensors can be reused throughout forward and backward computation with quantized storage, and HALO-2, which additionally applies left-hand-side Hadamard transformations to output gradients during input-gradient computation to further stabilize training under narrower dynamic-range formats such as INT8. The implementation combines tensor-wise symmetric quantization, fused Hadamard CUDA kernels, custom low-precision GEMM kernels, quantized activation storage for reduced memory usage, and an FSDP extension called HQ-FSDP that performs Hadamard transformations before communication, computes shared quantization scales across workers, and communicates quantized weight shards to reduce communication overhead. For parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the method precomputes and stores quantized Hadamard-transformed frozen weights while leaving the small low-rank adapter computations in high precision, allowing most computation to remain low precision without introducing significant overhead. Overall, the paper demonstrates that carefully placing orthogonal Hadamard transformations according to the observed structure of forward activations and backward gradients enables practical low-precision fine-tuning using simple tensor-wise quantization, avoiding the complexity of block-wise quantization while maintaining accuracy and improving computational efficiency.

title: Quartet: Native FP4 Training Can Be Optimal for Large Language Models
author: Roberto Castro et al
topic: quantization, qat, fp4, training
description: This paper introduces Quartet, a method for end-to-end native FP4 training of large language models that performs all major matrix multiplications directly in the hardware-supported MXFP4 format, demonstrating that FP4 can achieve a favorable accuracy-versus-computation tradeoff without relying on higher-precision fallbacks. The authors first derive a new scaling law that separates the effects of forward-pass precision and backward-pass precision into parameter efficiency and data efficiency, allowing different quantized training algorithms to be compared based on how much additional model size or training data is required to compensate for quantization error. Guided by this analysis, they identify that minimizing forward quantization error is best achieved using QuEST, which applies block-wise Hadamard transforms followed by optimized clipping and deterministic quantization, while the backward pass benefits from randomized block-wise Hadamard transforms combined with round-to-nearest MXFP4 quantization, striking a balance between quantization error and gradient bias rather than minimizing error alone. Their implementation keeps weights, activations, and gradients in higher precision outside the matrix multiplications but quantizes each operand immediately before GEMMs using fused CUDA kernels that combine Hadamard transforms, scale computation, clipping-mask generation, and MXFP4 conversion, then executes Blackwell-native block-scaled MXFP4 tensor core operations before dequantizing and inverting the transforms where necessary. To make this practical, they develop optimized CUTLASS-based kernels that exploit Blackwell’s native support for block-scaled MXFP4 arithmetic, carefully matching the hardware’s 32-element shared scaling layout while reorganizing scale tensors and fusing quantization operations to minimize memory traffic and overhead. The resulting system shows that combining theoretically motivated forward and backward quantization strategies with hardware-aware kernel design enables native FP4 training that preserves model quality while substantially increasing computational efficiency, suggesting that FP4 can become an effective training precision for future large-scale language models.

title: Efficient Data Selection at Scale via Influence Distillation
author: Mahdi Nikdan et al
topic: data, selection, influence functions, distillation
description: Influence Distillation introduces a theoretically grounded data selection framework that chooses training examples by estimating how much each sample will reduce loss on a target distribution after fine-tuning, replacing heuristic similarity metrics with an optimization objective derived from influence analysis. The method approximates the target loss after one optimization step using a second-order Taylor expansion, expressing the effect of weighted training samples as a quadratic function involving per-sample gradients, the target gradient, and the target Hessian, from which optimal sample weights can be analytically derived for both gradient descent and Adam before being regularized with non-negativity, normalization, and L2 constraints to produce stable, sparse selections. To make the approach practical for large language models, the authors observe that the second-order term is often negligible, allowing a first-order approximation that avoids Hessian computation, project gradients into a lower-dimensional space using randomized Hadamard transforms, and approximate gradients for most samples using only a small set of landmark examples. Specifically, they compute exact gradients only for landmark samples, fit coefficients that reconstruct every sample from landmark embeddings using kernel ridge regression, and transfer influence estimates through this low-rank approximation, while introducing Jacobian-vector product (JVP) embeddings that better preserve gradient relationships than conventional hidden-state embeddings by projecting intermediate network Jacobians onto random Gaussian directions. The regularization parameter controlling sparsity is automatically tuned with binary search so that exactly the desired number of samples receive nonzero weights, after which the selected subset is used for standard fine-tuning without retaining the learned weights themselves. Overall, the paper's main contribution is demonstrating that influence-based data selection can be made both mathematically principled and computationally efficient through analytical weight optimization, landmark-based gradient approximation, and JVP embeddings, enabling targeted fine-tuning with substantially lower selection cost while maintaining or improving downstream model quality.

title: Unified Scaling Laws for Compressed Representations
author: Andrei Panferov et al
topic: compression, scaling laws, quantization
description: This paper introduces a unified scaling law for training neural networks over compressed representations by replacing the raw parameter count with an effective parameter count N·ρ(R), where ρ(R) is a representation capacity that quantifies how efficiently a compression format preserves model expressiveness. The main implementation insight is that instead of fitting a separate scaling parameter for every compression configuration, the authors compute the Gaussian mean-squared error (GMSE) of a representation by measuring how accurately it reconstructs random Gaussian vectors, then map this error through a small parametric function to estimate ρ(R), allowing sparse, quantized, sparse-quantized, vector-quantized, and activation-compressed models to be analyzed within the same framework. Their theoretical analysis models compressed optimization with Adam and straight-through estimators, showing that optimization quality depends on the product of the model size and the average compression error, providing justification for why representation capacity is predictive of scaling behavior across different compression methods. They further demonstrate that representation capacities compose multiplicatively, meaning the capacity of combined compression schemes can be estimated as the product of the capacities of the individual components, making it possible to predict the behavior of complex compression pipelines without retraining every configuration. Building on this observation, they propose an improved sparse training algorithm called RMSE-Banded Backward Masking, which retains standard magnitude pruning during the forward pass but uses a separate backward gradient mask based on RMS-normalized parameter magnitudes to selectively block gradients within an adjustable band while allowing updates to both very small and very large weights, increasing effective representation capacity at the same sparsity level. Overall, the paper's primary contribution is showing that a simple intrinsic metric derived from Gaussian reconstruction error serves as a universal predictor of compressed model efficiency, enabling unified scaling analysis, analytical comparison of compression formats, accurate composition across multiple compression types, and improved sparse training algorithms.

title: SPEED: Sharpened-Teacher Distillation for Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
author: Qiuhong Shen et al
topic: dlm, parallel decoding, distillation
description: SPEED addresses the quality degradation that occurs when masked diffusion language models decode many tokens in parallel by reframing decoding as an iterative token grouping problem, arguing that errors arise because aggressively grouped tokens violate the conditional independence assumption and therefore rely on incomplete contextual information. To improve parallel decoding during training, the authors introduce Sharpened Teacher Distillation, where a frozen teacher generates predictions on partially masked blocks, and the student is optimized with a temperature-scaled KL divergence only on positions that the teacher already predicts correctly, while a standard masked language modeling loss over the entire active block preserves overall token accuracy. This selective distillation progressively concentrates probability mass on already-correct predictions, enabling more tokens to confidently exceed the decoding threshold without encouraging overconfident mistakes, and the teacher is periodically updated from the student to iteratively sharpen the supervision signal. During inference, the method introduces Slow–Fast Decoding, which computes a token-wise Jensen–Shannon Divergence (JSD) between each token's predictive distribution with and without access to previously decoded blocks, using this divergence as a measure of contextual sensitivity rather than relying solely on confidence scores. Tokens whose distributions remain relatively stable across contexts are grouped into a fast set and decoded aggressively in parallel, whereas context-sensitive tokens are temporarily deferred under a more conservative decoding strategy until additional neighboring tokens have been resolved, after which they are decoded using the standard threshold, all without requiring additional forward passes by reusing cached predictions from adjacent blocks. The paper's main contribution is the combination of confidence-sharpening distillation and JSD-based adaptive token grouping into a unified framework that enlarges safely decodable parallel groups, substantially reducing the number of sequential denoising steps while preserving generation quality, and it is designed to integrate with existing masked diffusion decoding pipelines with minimal implementation changes.

title: Singular Proxies for Adaptive Caching in Diffusion Language Models
author: Wenhao Sun et al
topic: dlm, svd, caching
description: SPA-Cache addresses the inference bottleneck of diffusion language models by introducing a training-free caching framework that reduces unnecessary hidden-state recomputation through more efficient update selection and adaptive computation allocation, rather than relying on heuristic locality assumptions or fixed update budgets. Its key insight is that the similarity of Value projections between consecutive denoising steps provides a theoretically justified proxy for determining whether a token's hidden state must be recomputed, supported by proofs showing that stable Value states bound changes in both the attention outputs and subsequent feed-forward outputs, making expensive full-layer recomputation unnecessary. To make this update identification practical, the authors perform a singular value decomposition of the Value projection matrix offline and retain only the leading singular directions, creating a low-dimensional "singular proxy" that approximates Value-space similarities while dramatically reducing the cost of projection and cosine similarity computations used to identify update-critical tokens. During decoding, each Transformer layer first projects input states into this compressed proxy space, selects the tokens with the largest estimated drift, recomputes attention queries, key/value states, and feed-forward outputs only for those selected tokens, and then scatters the updated representations back into the cached full-sequence states while all remaining tokens reuse their cached activations. In addition, the method replaces the conventional fixed update ratio across layers with an adaptive layer-dependent allocation based on the empirical observation that middle layers exhibit substantially greater hidden-state drift than early and late layers, allowing computation to be concentrated where updates are most beneficial while aggressively caching stable layers. Together, the low-dimensional singular proxy and adaptive update scheduling substantially reduce the overhead of cache management, are fully compatible with existing parallel decoding methods, and establish a more principled and computationally efficient framework for caching in diffusion language models.

title: dOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
author: Phuong Tuan Dat et al
topic: dlm, policy distillation, self-distillation
description: dOPSD introduces an on-policy self-distillation algorithm for diffusion language models that replaces the privileged information used in prior OPSD methods with information extracted directly from the model's own denoising trajectory, eliminating the need for external reference solutions while maintaining dense token-level supervision. The key insight is that during diffusion decoding, later denoising steps naturally contain more revealed context than earlier ones, so the same model can act as a stronger teacher by predicting masked tokens from these later intermediate states, creating an intrinsic "peek-ahead" advantage unique to diffusion decoding. Implementation begins by generating a complete on-policy decoding trajectory, randomly selecting an intermediate state that still contains many masked tokens, computing the student distribution only over those masked positions, then constructing the teacher target by averaging the model's predictions for the same positions across all future decoding steps in which they remain masked, and finally minimizing a stop-gradient Jensen-Shannon divergence between the student and this averaged teacher distribution. To ensure that the distilled supervision is reliable, the method verifies whether the final generated answer is correct and only applies the self-distillation loss to successful rollouts, while requiring no architectural modifications because both teacher and student use standard masked-prediction forward passes and differ only in which intermediate trajectory state they observe. The authors also identify two reasons why directly applying autoregressive OPSD to diffusion models fails: external privileged information collapses into a weak consensus policy because it is unavailable at inference time, and randomly masking completed sequences produces states that do not lie on the model's actual confidence-ordered decoding trajectory. Overall, the work demonstrates that treating the diffusion denoising trajectory itself as a source of privileged information yields an effective post-training objective that provides dense, on-policy supervision while remaining compatible with existing diffusion language model architectures and training pipelines.

title: The Geometry of LLM Quantization: GPTQ as Babai's Nearest Plane Algorithm
author: Jiale Chen et al
topic: quantization, post-training
description: This paper provides the first geometric interpretation of GPTQ by proving that weight quantization for a linear layer can be reformulated as a closest vector problem (CVP) on a lattice whose basis is determined by the layer activations and quantization scales, allowing the quantization process to be analyzed using classical lattice algorithms. The key theoretical result is that GPTQ, when executed in reverse dimension order, is mathematically identical to Babai’s nearest plane algorithm: each quantization step rounds one coordinate and then propagates the resulting error to the remaining coordinates, which the authors show is exactly equivalent to projecting a target vector onto the nearest lattice hyperplane. To establish this equivalence, they derive a correspondence between the GPTQ objective and CVP, reinterpret GPTQ’s Hessian-based error propagation as a geometric projection operation, and prove that the sequence of residual updates performed by GPTQ matches Babai’s recursive nearest-plane procedure. This perspective yields a tight layer-wise quantization error bound in the no-clipping setting, expressed through the diagonal terms of an LDL decomposition of the Hessian, and also explains how quantization order influences the final error through its effect on that decomposition. Building on the theory, the authors introduce practical no-clipping quantization methods: SSQR, which stores overflowed weights as sparse outliers while adjusting scales through binary search, and HPTQ, which quantizes onto an unrestricted integer lattice and uses Huffman coding to satisfy a target compression budget. They additionally implement optimized CUDA kernels for the resulting representations, demonstrating that the lattice-based interpretation is not only a theoretical framework but also a guide for designing more accurate and efficient post-training quantization algorithms.

title: SparseGPT: Massive Language Models Can be Accuracy Pruned in One-Shot
author: Elias Frantar et al
topic: pruning, post-training
description: SparseGPT introduces the first practical one-shot pruning method for massive GPT-style language models, showing that highly sparse models can be obtained without retraining by framing pruning as a layer-wise reconstruction problem that preserves each layer’s input-output behavior. The key contribution is a scalable approximation to Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS), a second-order pruning technique that uses the inverse Hessian of layer activations to estimate both the error incurred by removing a weight and the optimal compensatory update to the remaining weights. Direct OBS reconstruction is computationally infeasible because each row of a weight matrix would require solving a different sparse regression problem with its own masked Hessian inverse, so SparseGPT introduces Hessian synchronization, processing weights column-by-column while maintaining a shared sequence of inverse Hessians that can be updated efficiently through recursive Gaussian elimination rather than recomputed independently. During pruning, weights are removed according to a second-order saliency score proportional to the squared weight divided by the corresponding diagonal entry of the inverse Hessian, and after each removal the resulting error is propagated to later, still-unfrozen weights using OBS-style updates, allowing the network to continuously compensate for pruning damage. To avoid imposing rigid sparsity patterns and to account for weight correlations introduced by previous updates, the method performs adaptive mask selection in blocks, periodically recomputing which weights are cheapest to remove based on the evolving second-order error estimates. The algorithm is implemented in the same column-wise greedy framework as GPTQ, enabling efficient batched updates, numerically stable Cholesky-based inverse-Hessian computations, support for both unstructured and semi-structured sparsity patterns, and seamless integration of pruning and quantization into a single compression pass.

title: Statistically-Lossless Quantization for Large Language Models
author: Michael Helcig et al
topic: quantization, post-training
description: This paper introduces Statistically Lossless Quantization (SLQ), a framework that bridges the gap between conventional lossy quantization and exact lossless compression by defining two fidelity targets: task-lossless preservation of model behavior and the stricter distribution-lossless preservation of next-token distributions. A central contribution is the Expected Acceptance Rate (EAR), a token-level fidelity metric that measures the maximum probability that the original and quantized models produce the same token under optimal coupling, providing a more interpretable objective than KL divergence for quantization search. The authors also prove a gamma-squared variance law showing that symmetric quantization amplifies quantization noise by a factor proportional to the square of weight-distribution skewness, motivating the use of asymmetric quantization with learned zero-points as a prerequisite for high-fidelity distribution preservation. Their implementation quantizes each layer using asymmetric integer quantization while allowing a wide range of bitwidths from 2 to 8 bits, estimates layer sensitivities through a multi-bitwidth Shapley-value procedure, and builds a sensitivity database that predicts how each layer-bitwidth choice affects EAR and KL divergence. Given these sensitivity estimates, SLQ formulates bit allocation as an integer linear program that assigns bitwidths to layer groups under a compression budget, then performs a search to find the lowest average precision satisfying either an EAR constraint for distribution-lossless compression or a KL-derived recovery target for task-lossless compression. The resulting system combines asymmetric quantization, fine-grained mixed-precision allocation, Shapley-based sensitivity estimation, and optimization-driven bitwidth assignment to achieve highly compressed models that remain statistically indistinguishable from their original counterparts while retaining practical inference acceleration.

title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
author: Elias Frantar et al
topic: quantization, post-training
description: GPTQ presents a scalable post-training quantization method for large language models that achieves aggressive weight compression without retraining by approximating the effect of quantization using second-order information derived from layer activations. The method builds on Optimal Brain Quantization (OBQ), which quantizes weights while compensating for the resulting error using the inverse Hessian of the layer reconstruction objective, but replaces OBQ’s expensive greedy weight-by-weight ordering with a shared column-wise quantization order across all rows, exploiting the fact that the Hessian depends only on layer inputs and not on the weights themselves. This insight allows inverse-Hessian updates to be performed once per column rather than once per weight, reducing computational complexity by orders of magnitude while preserving most of the benefits of second-order error compensation. To make the algorithm practical on GPUs, GPTQ introduces lazy batch updates that quantize blocks of columns at a time, accumulate local quantization errors, and apply large matrix updates only after an entire block has been processed, significantly improving hardware utilization by reducing memory-bandwidth overhead. The authors further reformulate the algorithm using a damped Cholesky decomposition of the inverse Hessian, avoiding the numerical instability caused by repeated inverse updates while enabling efficient use of optimized linear algebra kernels. In implementation, GPTQ computes activation statistics from a small calibration set, constructs a layer-wise Hessian approximation, sequentially quantizes transformer layers using blockwise second-order error correction, and combines the resulting compressed weights with custom dequantization-aware inference kernels that reduce memory movement and translate compression into practical deployment and inference benefits.

title: ELF: Embedded Language Flows
author: Keya Hu et al
topic: dlm, continuous diffusion, consistency
description: The paper asks whether the underperformance of continuous diffusion language models is intrinsic to language discreteness or instead due to suboptimal design, and proposes Embedded Language Flows (ELF) to test the latter by removing most discrete constraints. ELF maps tokens into a continuous embedding space and performs generation entirely as a continuous-time flow matching process, where noisy embeddings follow a linear interpolant z_t = t x + (1 − t) ε and the model predicts clean embeddings x via an x-prediction objective that induces the correct velocity field. A key design choice is to avoid any token-level supervision during intermediate steps, allowing unconstrained trajectories in embedding space, and to defer discretization to a single final step implemented by a shared network that switches from denoising to decoding mode. This unification is technically important because predicting clean embeddings aligns the denoising objective with the final cross-entropy decoding loss, enabling weight sharing and eliminating the need for a separate decoder while preserving consistency between continuous and discrete representations. Because the model operates purely in continuous space until the end, it naturally supports techniques like classifier-free guidance and stochastic sampling, which improve controllability and error correction by modifying the learned velocity field during integration.

title: Where Should Diffusion Enter a Language Model? Geometry-Guided Hidden-State Replacement
author: Injin Kong et al
topic: dlm, diffusion models, geometry, hidden states
description: The paper asks where diffusion should be applied inside a pretrained transformer, hypothesizing that failure of continuous diffusion in language stems less from discreteness and more from using representation spaces with unfavorable geometry for denoising. It formalizes “diffusion-friendly” spaces via three properties—fast contraction under Langevin dynamics (linked to curvature), robustness to score estimation error (also controlled by curvature), and low effective dimensionality (captured by effective rank)—and derives these as practical spectral proxies computed layer-wise from hidden states. Using these proxies, it scores each transformer layer and selects an insertion point where hidden-state distributions are locally compact, globally well-conditioned, and lie near low-dimensional manifolds, making them easier targets for diffusion. The proposed DiHAL architecture then replaces the lower transformer layers with a conditional diffusion bridge trained to reconstruct the selected hidden state from noise, while keeping the upper layers and LM head unchanged so that token prediction is handled by the original autoregressive machinery. This design avoids unstable continuous-to-discrete recovery by shifting diffusion to an internal representation that the pretrained model already knows how to decode, effectively reframing language diffusion as hidden-state reconstruction in a geometrically suitable space.

title: SparseD: Sparse Attention for Diffusion Language Models
author: Zeqing Wang et al
topic: dlm, sparsity, attention
description: The paper addresses the high inference latency of diffusion language models by asking how to reduce the quadratic cost of bidirectional attention without breaking the denoising process. It observes that, unlike autoregressive models, attention in DLMs is head-specific but temporally stable across diffusion steps, and that early denoising steps are disproportionately important for forming correct global structure. Based on this, SparseD first runs full attention during early steps, then computes head-specific sparse attention patterns by selecting high-score query–key pairs (separately for prefill and generation tokens) using blockwise pooled attention, and reuses these fixed patterns for all subsequent steps. This works because the denoising trajectory stabilizes attention structure after early steps, so recomputing patterns each step is redundant, and restricting computation later does not significantly perturb the trajectory. The method reduces complexity by masking attention to a precomputed sparse set while preserving critical early global interactions, effectively amortizing the cost of pattern discovery and aligning sparsification with the temporal dynamics of diffusion.

title: Elastic-dLLM: Position Preserving Context Compression and Augmentation of Diffusion LLMs
author: Junyi Wu et al
topic: dlm, mask tokens, rope, context compression, iterative folding
description: The paper asks whether the large computational cost in diffusion language models comes from repeatedly processing many future [MASK] tokens that contribute little new information, and how to reduce this redundancy without breaking generation. It shows that although [MASK] tokens have highly redundant feature representations and mostly interact locally with each other, they encode critical structural signals through their RoPE positional indices, especially for determining where content should be generated and when to terminate. Based on this, the method compresses the future [MASK] context by sparsely sampling tokens from each block while keeping decoded history, the current block, and the terminal region dense, and crucially preserves each retained token’s original RoPE coordinate so that positional priors remain unchanged. This design works because generation in dLLMs is strongly guided by positional encoding rather than token identity for masked positions, so maintaining the positional “skeleton” preserves semantics even under heavy token reduction. The framework further extends to iterative folding, where older decoded tokens are also sparsified under the same positional-preserving rule for long-context scaling, and to block dLLMs by adding a single protected [MASK] token at the final RoPE position to explicitly reintroduce the terminal signal that guides EOS prediction.
